title: Between Orthodoxy and Reform: Theorizing the Suspension of Islamic Corporal Punishments in Shiʿi Theocracy

detail.title: Between Orthodoxy and Reform: Theorizing the Suspension of Islamic Corporal Punishments in Shiʿi Theocracy

keywords: The Occultation of the Twelfth Imam

detail.abstract: After the Occultation of the Twelfth Imam (al-ghaybah al-kubr a) in the fourth AH/tenth CE century, the applicability of divinely ordained punishments, _ hud ud, became a subject of theo-juridical controversies between two groups of Shiʿi jurists: pro-and anti-_ hud ud. In the aftermath of the Islamic Revolution of 1979 and the establishment of a Shiʿi theocracy, Iranian theocrats supported the pro-_ hud ud Shiʿi jurists, and as a result, _ hud ud punishments were incorporated into the Islamic Penal Code and have been applied by the state ever since. Some Iranian legal reformers, recognizing the challenges in applying _ hud ud punishments, have put forward two politico-juridical mechanisms (zarfiyat): the secondary ruling and the state order. These two mechanisms, the reformers assert, may be used by the Islamic Republic of Iran to suspend _ hud ud punishments. In this article, I examine both the arguments presented by reformers and the objections to these arguments raised by conservative and Shiʿi orthodox-minded jurists. These objections pose doctrinal challenges that impede the utilization of these mechanisms, thus obstructing the suspension of _ hud ud punishments.

title: Ascending versus Simultaneous Contests
affiliations: , Florida State University, Boise State University - Department of Economics and Florida State University

detail.title: Ascending versus Simultaneous Contests
detail.abstract: Lobbying was initially and remains a primary motivation for contest theory.  Real-world lobbying is often dynamic, but excepting the first contest experiment, the majority of such experiments are simultaneous-decision and almost always feature over-investment relative to theory.  Spurred by the disconnect between contest motivation and contest experimental design, we introduce a dynamic perturbation of the standard simultaneous contest called the Ascending Contest.  We compare behavior in this institution to behavior in the canonical experimental contest, to see if over-investment is at least partly an artifact of the latter's simultaneous design.  Surprisingly, we find no significant difference in aggregate investment across the two institutions.  Moreover, individual investment is distributed similarly in both settings.  When we examine individual investment in the Ascending Contest, we find little evidence of best-response behavior.  This result has implications for mutual best-response as a meaningful benchmark in simultaneous-decision contests.

detail.title: Childhood Vaccination Coverage and Health Indicators: Program Contract of the Andalusian Public Health System
detail.abstract: Objective: To analyse the relationship between childhood vaccination coverage in Andalusia and inclusion or exclusion in the programme contract of the Andalusian Public Health Service (SSPA). To analyse the relationship between childhood vaccination coverage included in the SSPA programme contract and the average vaccination coverage rates in Spain for the same vaccines and cohort years. Methodology: Original observational cross-sectional analytical study. Results: They confirm that vaccines included in the programme contract present significantly higher coverage rates than those excluded, also surpassing the national average for Spain. The study demonstrates strong internal and external validity, with Andalusia proving broadly comparable to other regions whilst retaining its own specific dynamics. Conclusions: This study allows us to establish an association between the inclusion of childhood vaccination coverage targets within healthcare centre outcome objectives at the regional level — as in the case of the SSPA — and higher vaccination coverage rates

title: Institutional Circuit Complexity: A Boolean Framework for the Efficiency-Incentive Tradeoff in Organizational Design
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Institutional Circuit Complexity: A Boolean Framework for the Efficiency-Incentive Tradeoff in Organizational Design
detail.abstract: We introduce the concept of Institutional Circuit Complexity (ICC) as a formal framework for measuring the structural complexity of economic organizations through the lens of Boolean algebra. We define any institution as a Boolean function f : {0,1}^n → {0,1} computed by a logic circuit, and prove that the gate complexity κ(f)the minimum number of logic gates required to evaluate collective decisionsacts as an endogenous lower bound on coordination costs and as a structural impediment to incentive-compatible mechanism design. Our main theorem establishes that institutions whose circuit complexity exceeds a critical threshold k* cannot simultaneously satisfy Dominant-Strategy Incentive Compatibility (DSIC) and Budget Balance (BB) under any transfer scheme. This result extends the classical Myerson-Satterthwaite impossibility to a purely structural dimension, independent of the type space. We derive corollaries for organizational design: AND-deep hierarchies face inherent IC constraints, while threshold-based voting rules achieve a Pareto-optimal tradeoff between coordination costs and strategic robustness. The framework unifies contributions from mechanism design, the theory of the firm, and computational complexity under a single algebraic roof.

detail.abstract:
Digital banking has transformed financial access in India but the benefits have not reached everyone equally. This study examines digital banking adoption and financial inclusion across urban, semi-urban and rural populations in India using primary survey data from 125 respondents collected through a structured online questionnaire. The study measures adoption patterns, evaluates the real-world impact of the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, identifies barriers to adoption and situates India's digital payment achievements within an honest global assessment.

The findings reveal a 1.27-point adoption gap between urban and rural respondents on a 5-point scale with rural users scoring below the neutral midpoint at 2.60. The Jan Dhan funnel shows 64.8% awareness dropping to 41.6% active usage confirming a significant dormancy problem. Multiple regression analysis explains 64.8% of variance in adoption outcomes with UPI usability as the strongest positive predictor and language barriers as the only significant negative predictor. One-way ANOVA confirms statistically significant differences across all three location types.

The study concludes that India has built world-class digital financial infrastructure but has not yet delivered meaningful inclusion to its most vulnerable populations. Fourteen tiered policy recommendations are offered addressing fraud communication, vernacular language mandates, Business Correspondent incentive reform and connectivity investment in underserved areas.

detail.title: The Large Role Small Businesses Play in Employment in New England
detail.abstract: Small businesses occupy a position of economic and civic importance in New England that is not captured by any single statistic. These firms collectively employ millions of workers, anchor local communities, supply large institutions with goods and services, and are incubators of regional innovation and job growth. Using data from the US Census Bureau’s Business Dynamics Statistics, this brief quantifies the contributions that small businesses made to employment and employment growth in New England during the 2000–2023 period.

title: Do Green Jobs Pay More? International Evidence Using the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Comptencies
affiliations: CAF Development Bank of Latin America, CAF Development Bank of Latin America, Carnegie Mellon University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Do Green Jobs Pay More? International Evidence Using the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Comptencies
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether green jobs pay higher wages than non-green jobs, and whether this differential persists once worker characteristics — including cog-nitive skills — are accounted for. Using the Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), we compare three Latin American economies with fourteen OECD countries divided into traditional and new mem-bers. We find a clear development gradient: the conditional green wage premium is large and stable in Latin America — around 22% — moderate but significant in new OECD member countries — around 6% — and vanishes entirely in traditional OECD economies once the full set of controls is included. Crucially, PIAAC-based controls play a quantitatively important role across all regions, reducing the esti-mated premium by between 10% and 20% even after standard controls are intro-duced — and eliminating its statistical significance entirely in traditional OECD economies, a result not visible with standard survey data. In Latin America, the premium is heavily concentrated among lower-wage workers and workers in small firms, suggesting that it largely reflects the precarious conditions of non-green employment rather than an exceptional return to green work per se. As a com-plementary finding, green jobs exhibit higher abstract task intensity and lower automation risk across all regions, even after controlling for individual skills.

title: Panel Local Projections without Fixed-Effects: A Cumulative-Difference OLS Estimator

detail.title: Panel Local Projections without Fixed-Effects: A Cumulative-Difference OLS Estimator
detail.abstract: Panel local projections have become a standard tool for estimating impulse response functions in empirical macroeconomics, yet their theoretical properties remain only partially understood. Recent work has shown that conventional fixed-effects estimators suffer from incidental-parameter (Nickell-type) bias, motivating analytical and jackknife bias corrections. This paper proposes a cumulative-difference OLS estimator for panel local projections that eliminates individual effects without relying on the within transformation. We show that cumulative differencing asymptotically removes the individual effects, derive the appropriate lag-augmented local projection specification, and prove that the resulting pooled OLS estimator is unbiased under standard exogeneity and stationarity assumptions. Monte Carlo simulations covering alternative persistence structures, sample dimensions, and dynamic specifications demonstrate that the proposed estimator consistently exhibits the smallest finite-sample bias and coverage probabilities close to their nominal levels, while the performance of fixed-effects, random-effects, and split-panel jackknife estimators depends critically on the persistence of both shocks and outcomes. Empirical applications further illustrate that estimator choice can materially affect estimated impulse responses. The results suggest that many biases recently documented in panel local projections arise from the interaction between within transformations and dynamic persistence rather than from local projections themselves, providing a simple and robust alternative for empirical researchers.

title: AFM-HiFormer: Medical Image Segmentation Based on Adaptive Fusion and Multi-Enhanced Hybrid Transformer

detail.title: AFM-HiFormer: Medical Image Segmentation Based on Adaptive Fusion and Multi-Enhanced Hybrid Transformer
detail.abstract: Medical image segmentation technology has become an important part of auxiliary diagnosis and lesion detection. However, existing convolutional neural networks and Transformer models still suffer from problems such as over-reliance on local features, blurred boundaries, and insufficient generalization in small sample scenarios. In this paper, a novel medical image segmentation network based on adaptive fusion and multi-enhanced hybrid Transformer (AFM-HiFormer) is proposed. By constructing a cross-scale heterogeneous feature interaction and adaptive fusion mechanism, the model achieves dynamic fusion of local and global features. The method realizes dynamic weight learning of multi-level features by designing adaptive multi-scale fusion modules combined with dilated convolution and feature enhancement mechanisms; introduces boundary perception and deep supervision mechanisms to improve segmentation accuracy for small organs and complex structures; and employs multiple data enhancement modules that integrate geometric, intensity, and other transformation strategies to enhance the generalization ability of the model. Experimental results on the Synapse dataset and the ACDC dataset show that the AFM-HiFormer model improves the Dice coefficient by about 4\%--5\% compared with mainstream methods and reduces the HD95 index by approximately 7\%, which fully verifies its advantages in the collaborative optimization of structural representation and data enhancement. This work provides a new idea for efficient medical image segmentation.

title: Completing the Curve: Visual Extrapolation and Short-term Return Predictability
affiliations: , Monash University and

detail.title: Completing the Curve: Visual Extrapolation and Short-term Return Predictability
detail.abstract: Humans automatically infer and complete unseen trajectories, shapes, and contours. We argue that this visual-completion tendency shapes investors' price beliefs and affects short-term asset prices. To isolate this channel, we use a computer vision model trained only on generic, non-financial images to inpaint the masked right-hand portion of stock price charts, mimicking visual completion while stripping away financial reasoning. Applying the model to approximately 16 million weekly U.S. price charts, we find a distinct impulse-correction pattern: model-implied returns positively predict next-day actual returns but negatively predict returns over the following days, consistent with visually induced overreaction and subsequent correction. This effect is stronger among small-cap, illiquid, and low-attention stocks, supporting a behavioral interpretation. Decomposition analysis shows that the completed segment nearest the visible history contains the strongest predictive signal, and that the predictability for next-day returns is concentrated overnight and decays from morning to afternoon. These findings suggest that human visual inference biases prices through a powerful but short-lived channel.

title: Does AI Crowd Out Context? Evidence from Clinical Radiology
affiliations: INSEAD and

detail.title: Does AI Crowd Out Context? Evidence from Clinical Radiology

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Human-AI collaboration is often deployed on the premise that algorithms provide precision while human decision makers provide contextual judgment. We identify a limit to this complementarity. AI advice can reduce the value that humans derive from contextual information the algorithm does not observe. We study this in an experiment in which radiologists evaluate chest X-ray cases with varied access to AI predictions and clinical history. Without AI, clinical history improves agreement with a fully informed benchmark most in cases where its measured value is greatest. When AI is displayed with clinical history, this relationship reverses, and the combined workflow moves farther from the benchmark precisely where clinical history should contribute most. A Bayesian signal-extraction framework shows that some reduction in the contribution of clinical history is rational when AI increases the precision of the image-based information. Yet the observed reduction of clinical-history value is roughly 2.6 times the calibrated Bayesian precision-reweighting benchmark. The loss appears across diagnostic ambiguity levels and all but the most skilled radiologist groups, suggesting that simple targeting rules are unlikely to eliminate it. Behavioral evidence suggests that AI changes attention rather than effort. Radiologists remain active but engage less with clinical history, and their assessments stay closer to the AI prediction. The findings show that the value of human contextual knowledge is endogenous to workflow design. AI advice can crowd out human contextual knowledge rather than simply complement it. Effective AI deployment depends not only on model accuracy, but also on when and how AI advice enters the decision process.

title: US-China Tariffs and Friendshoring in Pharmaceutical Global Value Chains
affiliations: Delhi Technological University - University School of Management and Entrepreneurship

detail.title: US-China Tariffs and Friendshoring in Pharmaceutical Global Value Chains
detail.abstract: This dissertation tries to examine whether US-China tariffs imposed from 2018 onward caused a significant shift in the US pharmaceutical imports from China towards India, a process termed friendshoring. Using bilateral HS3004 (medicaments) trade data across five major economies (2005-2024), the study combines network analysis of global value chain evolution with a triple difference-indifferences (DDD) identification strategy. The headline DDD estimate is 0.252 (SE = 0.190, p = 0.196), implying a 28.7 percent increase in US-India pharma imports attributable to tariffs, but statistically indistinguishable from zero at conventional significance levels. Event study analysis reveals strong pre-existing upward trends in US-India imports from at least 2013 onward, violating the parallel trends assumption required for causal identification. Compounding this, UN Comtrade data for US-China HS3004 imports are absent after 2012, making it impossible to directly observe the substitution channel the friendshoring hypothesis requires. The central finding is therefore a qualified null. That is, there is no statistically credible evidence that the 2018 tariffs caused a discrete acceleration in US pharmaceutical imports from India, beyond what pre-existing structural trends predict. Observed growth is better explained by India's generic drug industry expansion, driven by patent settlements, USFDA approval campaigns, and major US patent cliffs between 2010 and 2016, than by tariff-induced friendshoring. These findings will have direct implications for pharmaceutical supply chain policy, suggesting that tariffs on finished medicines are not adequately positioned to achieve supply chain diversification objectives and that upstream API-level interventions are where policy attention should be increasingly directed.

publicationDetails.detailsText: ADB Economics Working Paper Series No. 856

detail.abstract: This study explores the impact of subnational institutions on Viet Nam’s provincial manufacturing sector, comparing foreign-invested and domestic firms using a two-step difference GMM model with data from 63 provinces (2006–2020). Results show that changes in subnational institutions, measured by the Provincial Competitiveness Index, have little effect on economic complexity, revenues, employment, productivity, or firm size. Unexpectedly, weaker governance in areas like land access, transparency and legal institutions sometimes leads to better performance. This weak connection persists across all samples, periods, controls, and estimation methods, likely due to the dominance of foreign-invested companies and their limited interaction with local firms, which impacts overall firm development.

title: Option Prices and Option-Implied Probabilities in Incomplete Markets
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - Amsterdam School of Economics (ASE)

detail.title: Option Prices and Option-Implied Probabilities in Incomplete Markets
detail.abstract: This paper develops a methodology to quantify the uncertainty about option prices that persists in (statically) incomplete option markets due to finite strike and maturity grids as well as bid-ask price quoting. Uncertainty measures are provided for European option prices and their slopes (i.e., tail probabilities), each derived from model-free bounds that are consistent with a finite sample of observed bid and ask option prices and elementary no-arbitrage constraints in a multi-period setting. We obtain novel explicit expressions for these bounds, which are simple and efficient to compute. Moreover, we suggest a decomposition of the bounds and uncertainty measures into contributions of strike, maturity, and price quote incompleteness. In an empirical analysis of S&P 500 index options, we quantify the empirical uncertainty about option prices. We document sizable uncertainty levels for option prices and tail probabilities. Our findings challenge the common belief that such "option-implied" (tail) information can be measured at sufficiently high precision, which has implications for many empirical asset pricing applications that use this information.

detail.abstract:
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) in Nepal has undergone a significant transformation over the past two decades, evolving from isolated philanthropic initiatives, such as occasional donations to schools, religious institutions, and disaster relief efforts, into a more structured and policy-oriented approach to responsible business. This article critically examines this evolution, particularly in the context of the twentieth anniversary of the National Business Initiative (NBI), as a moment to reflect on the progress, challenges, and future direction of CSR in Nepal. The study argues that CSR discourse has gradually shifted from a charity-based orientation towards strategic responsibility, sustainability, and collective impact, influenced by Nepal’s political transitions, economic liberalisation, and increasing alignment with global governance and sustainability standards. However, despite this progress, CSR practices continue to face challenges arising from institutional fragmentation, compliance-driven mind-sets, and weak implementation mechanisms, resulting in a persistent gap between organisational intentions and societal outcomes.

The article highlights that the transition from fragmented giving to collective impact represents more than an operational change; it signifies a fundamental rethinking of the role of business as a partner in addressing social and developmental challenges. It concludes that strengthening institutional collaboration, embedding sustainability principles, and fostering shared responsibility among businesses, government, and communities are essential for advancing Nepal’s responsible business movement towards meaningful and inclusive impact.

title: Data Scraping, Artificial Intelligence, and Human Rights: Challenges for Africa

detail.title: Data Scraping, Artificial Intelligence, and Human Rights: Challenges for Africa
detail.abstract: Human rights doctrine recognizes the protection of the rights and freedoms of every bona fide citizen as a fundamental obligation of the state, enforced through constitutional, statutory, and international legal instruments. However, the rapid emergence and adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies across in a developing continent like Africa countries,have introduced challenges to the protection of these rights, particularly the right to privacy and data protection. While AI offers substantial benefits for economic growth, innovation, and public service delivery, its increasing reliance on data scraping has raised serious concerns regarding the unauthorized collection and processing of personal information.In many instances, AI-driven data scraping is conducted without the informed consent of data subjects, resulting in practices that may infringe fundamental human rights and undermine existing privacy and data protection laws. Such activities can be intrusive, objectionable, and harmful to individuals, especially where scrapers operate with little regard for legal or ethical standards. Although privacy rights are not absolute and exceptions may exist in circumstances such as public interest, law enforcement, or legitimate research purposes, these exceptions must be narrowly interpreted and applied within established legal frameworks. This article examines the intersection of data scraping, artificial intelligence, and human rights in the Africa. It explores the legal exceptions to privacy protections, analyses the challenges posed by AI-enabled data scraping, and assesses the adequacy of existing regulatory frameworks across African states. The article further proposes strategies for strengthening privacy and data protection regimes to safeguard individual rights while promoting responsible AI innovation and preventing unlawful data scraping practices.

title: Sustainability-Related Financial Information and Valuation. A Case Study of Vale
affiliations: University of São Paulo - School of Economics, Business and Accounting and University of São Paulo (USP)

detail.title: Sustainability-Related Financial Information and Valuation. A Case Study of Vale
detail.abstract: The adoption of IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 has expanded the set of sustainability-related financial information available to capital providers and renewed the debate on the effective use of such content in fundamental analysis and in the improvement of predictive accuracy. This study explores how the sustainability-related financial information reports issued by Vale S.A. for the 2024 and 2025 fiscal years can be combined with the financial statements of the same periods to support revenue, cost and expense projections, the assessment of risks and opportunities, and the refinement of the forecast horizon and the discount rate within a valuation process. The methodological approach is a single qualitative case study based on documentary triangulation. The theoretical framework draws on voluntary disclosure theory, the literature on the informational relevance of climate risk, and the empirical evidence linking sustainability disclosure to analyst forecast accuracy. The findings reveal verifiable connectivity between climate disclosure and critical accounting estimates, notably the sensitivity analysis of asset recoverable amounts disclosed in Note 17 of the 2025 financial statements. Ten propositions are formulated that connect disclosed items to accounting line items and to discounted cash flow parameters, and the incorporation of this information into free cash flow to the firm and free cash flow to equity is discussed.

detail.title: Research Integrity in Academic Publishing: The TRUST Framework for Navigating Ethical Uncertainty

publicationDetails.detailsText: Communications of the Association for Information Systems, 58, 49–80, 2026. DOI: 10.17705/1CAIS.05804

detail.abstract: Academic publishing norms are being actively renegotiated. Generative AI, growing expectations for transparency in authorship and contribution, and heightened attention to conflicts of interest in peer review have made ethical ambiguities more visible, while existing rules and guidelines often address them only partially. Doctoral students and early-career scholars are especially exposed to these grey areas, yet access to trusted, practice-based guidance remains uneven. To address this gap, a mentorship panel organised through the AIS Doctoral Student College brought together senior Information Systems scholars and doctoral students to discuss concrete ethical scenarios in academic publishing. Across two global online sessions, 192 participants from 30 countries engaged in discussions in which eight senior scholars responded to participant-submitted scenarios on plagiarism, generative AI in research, and conflicts of interest in peer review. The sessions generated 28 practical takeaways and a consistent cross-cutting message: ethical publishing requires not only technical compliance with rules, but also transparency, scholarly honesty, and a sustained commitment to research integrity. Building on these insights, this report introduces the TRUST framework-Transparency, Responsibility, Understanding, Support, and Timeliness-as practical guidance for navigating ethical grey areas in academic publishing. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.17705/1CAIS.05804

detail.abstract: This working paper synthesizes three usually disconnected bodies of literature-the political economy of the developmental state, studies on economic affirmative action, and the management literature on Base of the Pyramid (BoP) entrepreneurship-to answer a single question: under what conditions do private sector promotion policies strengthen an entrepreneurial class among the poorest in emerging markets, rather than consolidating already established elites or producing state-dependent rentiers? The central argument is that the decisive factor is neither the volume of support nor the chosen instrument (identity-based or universal, micro or macro), but the institutional structure of incentives-in Baumol's formulation, that determines whether entrepreneurial talent is allocated to production or to rent-seeking. The paper covers the macro axis (Evans, Amsden, Schneider; evidence on BNDES), the axis of inclusion of subordinated groups (Malaysia, South Africa, Indonesia; the Aymara bourgeoisie in Bolivia), and the micro axis (enablers, mechanisms of ascent, contradictions, and difficulties of BoP entrepreneurship). It concludes that the three levels converge on the same diagnosis and identifies, as a main gap and potential contribution, the absence of an articulation between macro-structural analysis and the question of who-in terms of social and racial origin-effectively ascends.

title: "If Not Certain Be Vague": How Uncertainty about Investors' Preferences Shapes Voluntary Climate-Change Disclosure
affiliations: and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: "If Not Certain Be Vague": How Uncertainty about Investors' Preferences Shapes Voluntary Climate-Change Disclosure
detail.abstract: Utilizing the unique setting of the CDP (previously, the Carbon Disclosure Project), we investigate the role of uncertainty about investors' preferences in voluntary climate change-related disclosure. We examine whether firms choose to remain silent and vague to mitigate potential dissatisfaction among investors when uncertain of how the voluntary disclosure will be perceived. We provide evidence that uncertainty about investors' environmental preferences is positively related to silence and vagueness in voluntary climate-change disclosure using both dictionary-based and ClimateBERT-based measures. Moreover, we show that companies with extreme environmental performance (either extremely "bad" or extremely "good") are more silent and vague in their disclosure when facing uncertain institutional investors' preferences. Additional analyses indicate that this association is incremental to general public opinion about climate change. Finally, the level of silence and vagueness in the previous year is positively associated with analysts' climatechange interest during Q&A sessions of earnings calls. Overall, the paper sheds light on a potential explanation for the persistent prevalence of silence and boilerplate sustainability disclosure.

title: Freezing Assets Before Judgment: A Brazilian Case Study on Proportionality, Due Process, and Hybrid Anti-Corruption Enforcement

detail.title: Freezing Assets Before Judgment: A Brazilian Case Study on Proportionality, Due Process, and Hybrid Anti-Corruption Enforcement
detail.abstract: This article examines pre-judgment asset freezing in corporate anti-corruption cases through the lens of Brazilian anti-corruption enforcement. The asset-freezing mechanism provided by Article 19(4) of Brazilian Law No. 12,846/2013the Brazilian Clean Company Actis not treated merely as a domestic procedural issue, but as an expression of a broader problem: how legal systems can preserve assets, secure compensation, and ensure the effectiveness of corporate anti-corruption enforcement without converting interim measures into anticipated punishment. Brazil offers a particularly relevant case study because its model combines negotiated, administrative, and judicial mechanisms: leniency agreements, administrative liability proceedings, judicial actions, multiple enforcement authorities, and court-controlled patrimonial restraints. This architecture does not fully reproduce foreign negotiated enforcement models, such as the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act model, nor does it operate as a purely adjudicatory system. It is better described as a hybrid model: increasingly coordinated in the federal consensual sphere, yet still dependent on administrative and judicial adjudication. The article argues that the legitimacy of anti-corruption asset freezing depends on a calibration matrix composed of qualified evidence of the harmful act, corporate interest or benefit, economic delimitation of the measure, individualized reasoning, preservation of lawful business continuity, consideration of cooperation and integrity programs, admissibility of substitute guarantees, periodic review, and interinstitutional coordination. Recent Brazilian developmentsespecially the CGU/AGU Interministerial Normative Ordinance No. 1/2025 and the CGU Guide for Identifying and Quantifying the Advantage Obtained-reinforce the article's thesis: the Brazilian State has begun to rationalize negotiated enforcement, but judicial asset-freezing still requires a corresponding methodology. The article concludes that Brazilian anti-corruption asset freezing should pursue effectiveness without automatic restraint, statutory autonomy without arbitrariness, and patrimonial preservation without anticipated punishment.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how household credit dynamics are associated with real house price growth across OECD economies. Using an annual country-level panel for 1995–2024 that combines OECD house price indicators, World Bank macroeconomic controls, BIS household credit data, BIS debt service ratios, and BIS central bank policy rates, the paper documents a robust stock-flow credit pattern. Lagged household credit growth is positively associated with short-run real house price growth, whereas the lagged stock of household credit is negatively associated with subsequent growth. These patterns remain visible across alternative clustering schemes, sample restrictions, and outlier treatments. By contrast, annual observed policy-rate measures do not display comparably robust independent associations once country and year fixed effects are included. Local projections indicate that the positive credit-growth association is concentrated at short horizons and becomes statistically imprecise at longer horizons. The evidence is therefore consistent with a macrofinancial housing mechanism in which new borrowing supports short-run demand, while accumulated leverage may constrain future appreciation. The estimates should be interpreted as robust conditional associations rather than causal effects.

title: Two Cooperative Systems, One Mission: A Comparative Analysis of Canadian and United States Credit Unions
affiliations: Bellevue University

detail.title: Two Cooperative Systems, One Mission: A Comparative Analysis of Canadian and United States Credit Unions
detail.abstract: The credit union movement represents one of the most enduring and successful examples of cooperative finance in the modern economy. Originating from nineteenth-century European social and economic reform movements, credit unions were established to provide affordable financial services to individuals and communities that were often underserved by traditional banking institutions. Over time, these member-owned financial cooperatives evolved into sophisticated organizations capable of delivering a full range of consumer, commercial, and investment services while maintaining their commitment to democratic governance, community development, and financial inclusion. Among the world's most successful cooperative financial systems are those found in Canada and the United States. Although these systems share common philosophical foundations, they have developed within distinct historical, regulatory, and economic environments that have shaped their organizational structures, strategic priorities, and approaches to serving members. This article examines the similarities and differences between Canadian and United States credit unions through a comprehensive comparative analysis of their historical development, cooperative philosophy, governance structures, regulatory frameworks, financial operations, commercial lending activities, technological innovation, organizational cultures, and future strategic challenges. Particular attention is given to the role credit unions play in promoting economic development, supporting small businesses, enhancing financial inclusion, and maintaining strong community relationships while competing against traditional banks and emerging financial technology companies. The analysis argues that Canadian and American credit unions represent two evolutionary paths of the same cooperative movement rather than fundamentally different institutional models. Their differences largely reflect the legal, political, and economic circumstances under which they developed, while their similarities demonstrate the enduring relevance of cooperative principles in contemporary financial services. The article concludes that the future success of both systems will depend upon effective governance, strategic leadership, prudent risk management, technological innovation, and the continued ability to balance financial sustainability with cooperative values and member-focused service.

title: Airport Problems with Cloned Agents
affiliations: Universidade de Vigo, University of Vigo, Universidade de Vigo - Departamento de Matemáticas and University of Vigo

detail.title: Airport Problems with Cloned Agents
detail.abstract: In an airport problem, a group of agents are clones of each other if they have the same cost parameter. For a problem with cloned agents, we present a thorough description of the structure of the set of contribution vectors that satisfy the no-subsidy constraints. We provide simplified formulae to compute the basic rules in terms of the different cost parameters and the number of cloned agents in each group. For several rules, this formulation is given by a weighted version of the rule. Remarkably, the core-center rule can be computed as the expected value of the conditional distribution of a Dirichlet distribution with parameters given by the number of clones in each group. Finally, we study if the basic rules are invariant or if they converge under replication to another rule.

title: Ansoff's Strategic Posturing in Turbulent Environments
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice, Department of Management, Students

detail.title: Ansoff's Strategic Posturing in Turbulent Environments
detail.abstract: We test whether Ansoff's Strategic Success Hypothesis (SSH) holds when operationalized as a measurable strategic posture diagnostic and linked to cash-based performance under turbulence. The goal is to provide a managerially usable alignment metric that is empirically validated. Design/methodology/approach We assemble a 10-year panel of 107 Nasdaq-listed firms (2006-2015). Strategic posture (X₁) is derived from the OSPP diagnostic; performance is year-over-year operating cash-flow growth (X₃). We estimate posture-performance associations and report extensive diagnostics and intercoder checks. Findings Strategic posture is positively and significantly associated with operating cash-flow growth. Effect sizes are modest but robust to alternative functional forms and diagnostics, consistent with a severe single-predictor test on a volatile cash outcome. Research limitations/implications Evidence comes from large U.S. firms; the main single-coder panel is complemented by intercoder studies. Results establish a quantitative baseline for like-for-like replications and extensions to other outcomes, geographies, and turbulence regimes. Practical implications The OSPP-based posture score supports a four-step cycle (measure-benchmark-diagnoseadjust), enabling proactive alignment management in turbulent environments. Originality This is the first large-sample, cash-flow-based validation of SSH using the OSPP posture diagnostic. It advances SSH from concept to testable diagnostic and provides instruments/datasets for replication.

title: A 30-Minute Board-CEO Conversation for Making Strategy Executable: The CEO Profile Workbook (CUP-W)
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice, Department of Management, Students

detail.title: A 30-Minute Board-CEO Conversation for Making Strategy Executable: The CEO Profile Workbook (CUP-W)
detail.abstract: Boards and CEOs frequently discuss strategy without a shared, explicit understanding of three conditions that strongly shape execution: how the CEO approaches risk and time horizon, what the CEO can realistically decide without escalation, and the level of pressure and complexity currently borne by the role. When these conditions remain implicit, boards experience late surprises while CEOs experience friction, delays, and misaligned oversight. This article introduces a practical, time-efficient tool designed to surface and align these conditions in a single, structured conversation. Design/methodology/approach The article introduces the CEO Upper Echelon Profile Workbook (CUP-W), a structured conversation scaffold that can be implemented in approximately 30 minutes. CUP-W combines short, anchored prompts covering executive orientation, perceived managerial discretion, and executive job demands with two brief decision vignettes. The tool is illustrated through five core CEO conversations and one later contrast case conducted across four countries and multiple industries, supplemented by brief documentary checks and cross-case comparison. Insights Using the same tool across different contexts shows that identical stated risk appetites translate into very different strategic behaviors depending on discretion and demands. When discretion and demands are both high, CEOs tend to act boldly but rely on explicit guardrails such as milestones and pilots. When demands are high but discretion is more constrained, risk-taking is translated into stage-gated execution and consensus-building. When discretion is structurally limited by governance arrangements, strategic action shifts toward adjacent or incremental initiatives rather than large-scale transformation. Originality/value CUP-W translates established research on executive decision making into a repeatable boardroom routine, the output is a concise, one-page CEO context profile and an explicit set of governance guardrails that boards and executive teams can implement immediately to improve strategic alignment and execution.

title: Safe Strategies in Multi-Unit Auctions: Equilibria, Liquid Welfare, and Revenue
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Operations Research Center

detail.title: Safe Strategies in Multi-Unit Auctions: Equilibria, Liquid Welfare, and Revenue
detail.abstract:
Multi-unit auctions are widely used to allocate scarce resources in markets such as Treasury, electricity, and emissions permits. In this work, we study the market implications when return-on-investment (RoI)-constrained value-maximizing bidders follow safe strategies (Golrezaei and Sahoo, 2025) in two popular multi-unit formats: (i) uniform-price (UP) and (ii) pay-as-bid (PAB) auctions. Safe strategies are those that guarantee RoI feasibility irrespective of competing bids. They satisfy mild no-overbidding conditions, admit polynomial-time no-regret learning in the online setting, and are provably robust against much richer classes of bidding strategies. We first characterize safe strategies for PAB auctions, complementing the result of Golrezaei and Sahoo (2025) for UP auctions. To show the existence of pure Nash equilibrium (PNE) in safe strategies, we introduce the notion of characteristic equilibrium (ChE): a unique, auction-independent PNE with simple and desirable structural properties. 
We give a constructive proof of the existence of a PNE by proposing an O(nK)-time algorithm, SLIP (Sequential Local Improvement via max-Priority), that computes the ChE, where n is the number of bidders and K is the number of units. The convergence of SLIP follows via an index-based potential function argument. We then show that every PNE in safe strategies can be mapped to a ChE. Moreover, we quantify equilibrium inefficiency via the liquid price of anarchy and prove a tight bound of 2 for both formats. 
Finally, we investigate the implications of equilibrium multiplicity for the market participants. We show that all PNE in safe strategies induce the same allocation; consequently, bidders aiming to maximize their liquid welfare are indifferent among all equilibria. In contrast, the seller's revenue can fluctuate significantly. We prove that the ChE maximizes revenue among equilibria. Then, we define the equilibrium revenue gap (ERG) of an auction format as the worst-case ratio of the maximum and minimum equilibrium revenue of an instance, over all instances. For UP auctions, ERG can scale with K in general, but improves to 2 under mild competition conditions. For PAB auctions, ERG is always at most 2. Furthermore, all ERG bounds are tight.

title: Status and Trends of Unfunded Liabilities of State and Local Pension Funds 2024
affiliations: Stanford University - Hoover Institution

detail.title: Status and Trends of Unfunded Liabilities of State and Local Pension Funds 2024
detail.abstract: Unfunded pension obligations are the largest liability on the balance sheets of U.S. state and local governments, yet prevailing actuarial standards understate their true economic size. This study assesses the status of U.S. public pension systems at the close of fiscal year 2024, using a sample that covers more than 90% of public pension assets across states, cities, and counties, and valuing liabilities both as reported and on a market basis. The distinction is consequential: governments report unfunded liabilities of $1.532 trillion, but a market-based valuation puts the shortfall at $4.009 trillion. The aggregate funding ratio falls accordingly, from a reported 77.7% to 57.1% under market valuation. This gap is driven by discount rates: assumed returns remained stagnant at 6.9%, far above the duration-matched, risk-equivalent market rate of 4.3%, leaving both the unfunded liability and the annual cost of newly accruing benefits substantially understated. Fiscal year 2024 was nonetheless a year of improvement: rising market rates and strong asset returns of 9.4% lifted funding ratios, and contributions are at 27.4% of payroll, exceeding the market-based cost of new accruals for a third consecutive year. Even so, contributions remain well short of what would be required merely to keep the unfunded liability from growing-an additional $71.8 billion in contributions would be required annually. Absent an alignment of assumed and market-based discount rates, the scale of pension obligations, and the risk they pose to their sponsors, will remain obscured.

detail.abstract: Environmental sustainability started to flourish across social science during the nineties. Thus, academic literature has provided a conceptual landscape of Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) topic. However, to date, few researchers have shed light on GHRM measurement that was mentioned in the literature. Such measurement lacks the scientific development and testing that reveal GHRM construct. This research aims to develop and test scientifically-based multi-items construct that empirically reflects the main dimensions and items of GHRM. Therefore, the authors will follow the steps of the scale development process that could produce more valid and reliable multi-item scale of GHRM. In this research, four studies will be conducted to confirm the developed scale's validity and reliability. Moreover, this research will be an aid to top management and HR managers in using the right items of GHRM to develop and implement environmental sustainability strategies.

title: The Forgotten Core of the Father of Strategic Management: Revisiting the Ansoff-Mintzberg Debate and the Strategic Success Hypothesis Purpose
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice, Department of Management, Students

detail.title: The Forgotten Core of the Father of Strategic Management: Revisiting the Ansoff-Mintzberg Debate and the Strategic Success Hypothesis Purpose
detail.abstract: This paper reconstructs the Ansoff-Mintzberg exchange as a historically significant contingency truce rather than a winner-loser outcome. It argues that the debate's enduring legacy is the unresolved question of strategic correctness: when firms should converge toward prevailing industry norms and when they should diverge in pursuit of strategic becoming. From this perspective, the paper repositions Igor Ansoff as a pioneer whose most consequential contribution-the Strategic Success Hypothesis (SSH)-was gradually marginalized, fragmented in later research and left only partially validated for decades.

title: Becoming an Agentic Enterprise: A Practitioner Methodology & Frameworks for Human-AI Governance

detail.title: Becoming an Agentic Enterprise: A Practitioner Methodology & Frameworks for Human-AI Governance
detail.abstract:
The transition from pilot projects to enterprise-scale autonomous AI systems represents one of the most significant governance challenges facing organizations today. While much attention has focused on the technical capabilities of large language models and agentic systems, comparatively little research has addressed the practical governance frameworks and methodology required to manage portfolios of agents at scale within an Enterprise. This creates a governance gap that keeps enterprises in long pilot cycles. For enterprises to confidently deploy, they need governing frameworks: Boards lack comprehensive frameworks to assess, classify, and oversee these increasingly sophisticated human-algorithm systems. Transformation leaders need a way to assess the human oversight required as agent complexity evolves.

This paper introduces the “Becoming an Agentic Enterprise” methodology developed by the author (s) as a comprehensive practitioner framework, grounded in direct engagement with enterprise transformation initiatives. The methodology comprises four interlocking components: SCORE-AI for board-level governance assessment, the L1-L6 Agent Maturity Model for capability classification, the AURA framework for human oversight calibration & the extent of integration required with existing systems and processes, and the RRR transformation sequence for phased implementation. We illustrate the application of this integrated methodology through a detailed case study of an enterprise software company that uses this framework, resulting in a blueprint for ~100 agents across eight business domains spanning the spectrum of agent maturity. The paper contributes to the human-AI interaction literature by demonstrating how layered governance structures can maintain meaningful human oversight while enabling operational autonomy, and by providing a replicable blueprint for enterprise-scale agentic transformation.

This paper addresses the HAI Workshop 2026 theme of 'Shaping the future of AI: innovation, ethics and impact' by:

(1) Innovation: Proposing novel frameworks (SCORE-AI, L1-L6, AURA) for classifying and governing agentic AI systems across enterprises

(2) Ethics: Embedding oversight through the SCORE-AI Ethics pillar and human oversight calibration at the agent level 
(3) AI Impact: Offering a practitioner-developed methodology for boards navigating AI governance.

title: Stable Matching with Shortlists: The Cost of (A Little) Preference Correlation
affiliations: Tsinghua University, School of Economics & Management, Students, National University of Singapore (NUS) and Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management

detail.title: Stable Matching with Shortlists: The Cost of (A Little) Preference Correlation
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Large matching platforms often cap how many partners an agent can rank because of the operational cost of eliciting full rankings. Under independent and uniform preferences, prior work suggests that nearly perfect stable matchings can be achieved even from shortlisted (top-k) information. We ask whether this conclusion persists when preferences become correlated, as is typical in platforms with skewed popularity.
Methodology: We introduce a hierarchical Plackett-Luce model for random preferences. Each agent's ranking is always marginally uniform over all permutations while the strength of correlation is controlled by the realized attraction scores. Using this model, we quantify preference correlation using standard rank measures such as Kendall's τ and Spearman's ρ, and study the matching outcomes generated by the standard top-k deferred acceptance algorithm, using submitted-list coverage to explain when many agents remain unmatched.
Results: We establish a lower bound that links shortlist length, preference correlation, and market efficiency. In particular, as the market size n grows, the expected number of unmatched agents can remain Θ(n) even when preferences are asymptotically uncorrelated and shortlist length scales as k = n α for any α < 1. This contrasts sharply with the independent setting, where Õ(1)length shortlists can ensure that only O(1) agents are unmatched.
Managerial implications: Even mild preference correlation can lead to severe congestion and market inefficiency. Hence, platforms should not rely on "just let users list more options." Instead, platforms could manage exposure: our numerical results indicate that simple assortment policies, including random-k assortment and tier-aware-k assortment, can substantially reduce unmatched rates while keeping information requirements low.

title: How Structured Process-Improvement Practices Influence Productivity in Hybrid Nonprofit Community Health Organizations

detail.title: How Structured Process-Improvement Practices Influence Productivity in Hybrid Nonprofit Community Health Organizations
detail.abstract: Hybrid nonprofit community health organizations face persistent productivity inefficiencies as they coordinate work across on-site and remote staff under workforce shortages, rising service demand, and strict funding accountability. Although hybrid work is often blamed for these inefficiencies, the underlying cause is contested. The purpose of this Rapid Evidence Assessment (REA) was to examine how structured process-improvement practices influence workflow efficiency and productivity outcomes in hybrid nonprofit community health settings, using Operations Management Theory as theoretical lens. Following the Center for Evidence-Based Management (CEBMa) protocol, peer-reviewed evidence published from 2019 to 2026 was systematically retrieved, screened, and appraised with the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) Qualitative Checklist, and synthesized through thematic synthesis in ATLAS.ti. Fifteen studies met the final criteria. The synthesis produced four themes: hybrid conditions intensify workflow-coordination barriers when integrating systems are absent; process inconsistency drives productivity inefficiency; clear accountability structures strengthen operational responsiveness; and structured process-improvement practices enhance productivity. The evidence indicates that productivity inefficiencies arise primarily from fragmented operational systems rather than from hybrid work arrangements themselves. Grounded in Operations Management Theory, the study reframes hybrid productivity challenges as operational-systems problems and offers four prioritized, theory-aligned recommendations for nonprofit managers.

title: CVaR-Constrained Revenue Optimization in Supply Chain Finance: A Stochastic Mixed-Integer Programming Framework with Scenario-Based Risk Decomposition

detail.title: CVaR-Constrained Revenue Optimization in Supply Chain Finance: A Stochastic Mixed-Integer Programming Framework with Scenario-Based Risk Decomposition
detail.abstract: We present a stochastic mixed-integer programming (SMIP) framework for revenue optimization in business-to-business supply chain finance, where decision-makers must simultaneously allocate logistics actions across a portfolio of shipments subject to uncertainty in revenue, cost, delay penalties, and credit loss. The central contribution is the Enterprise Financial Index (EFI), a unified scalar objective defined as EFI = E[V]-lambda * |min(0, CVaR_alpha)|, where V = R-C-P-L is the net outcome per scenario, E[V] is the scenario-weighted expectation, CVaR_alpha is the Conditional Value-at-Risk at confidence level alpha, and lambda is a risk-aversion parameter. This formulation is embedded as the per-shipment coefficient in a binary integer program that selects one action per shipment subject to a global capital budget constraint, solved via OR-Tools SCIP with a deterministic time bound. We introduce a three-regime risk-appetite parameterization (Conservative: lambda=2.0, alpha=0.05; Balanced: lambda=1.0, alpha=0.15; Aggressive: lambda=0.3, alpha=0.35) and demonstrate that the optimal action selection changes materially across regimes for shipments with high-variance cost structures. The framework further extends the base EFI to a Total Landed Cost (TLC) formulation incorporating import duties, tariff risk, demurrage, holding costs, and opportunity costs. Numerical results on synthetic supply chain scenarios show that CVaR-penalized optimization recovers 12-18% additional tail-risk protection relative to naive expected-value maximization, with less than 3% reduction in expected EFI under the balanced regime. The framework is deployed within Fiscalogix, a deterministic AI platform for autonomous supply chain finance, and integrates with an upstream AR default model and a downstream multi-agent execution layer.

detail.abstract:
This paper responds to Kello et al. (2026), "Building NHS Resilience to Ransomware: Central Oversight and Shared Capability" (King's College London Cyber Security Research Group). The response does not challenge the white paper's diagnosis – that inconsistent implementation rather than absent knowledge drives NHS ransomware vulnerability – but extends it by identifying structural failure modes in the proposed governance architecture.

Drawing on cross-sectional analysis of 171 NHS Trusts and the author’s research programme in governance architecture and institutional decision-making, the response advances four arguments. First, the white paper diagnoses compliance-as-illusion, then prescribes static measurement instruments that reproduce the same illusion at scale; velocity-based alternatives – measuring improvement rate rather than positional attainment – are more appropriate to an adaptive threat environment. Second, board literacy interventions are necessary but insufficient without redesigning the communication channel through which risk information reaches the board; high-context institutional norms systematically degrade urgency signals in transit. Third, centralisation creates a coordination-cost bottleneck subject to the same non-linear dynamics that defeated NPfIT; work-in-progress constraints and staged sequencing are required. Fourth, the strongest justification for centralisation lies not in enforcing uniform compliance, but in operating the threat intelligence function – already active in NHS England's CSOC/TISP – that gives distributed local improvement a directional signal.

The paper concludes with a collaborative research agenda identifying five questions that neither the KCL team's qualitative evidence base nor the author’s programme's quantitative analysis can answer alone.

title: Mega Development Projects, Growth, and Human Development: Project-Level Evidence, Sectoral Heterogeneity, Convergence Dynamics, and the Hydrogen Horizon (1960-2026)

detail.title: Mega Development Projects, Growth, and Human Development: Project-Level Evidence, Sectoral Heterogeneity, Convergence Dynamics, and the Hydrogen Horizon (1960-2026)
detail.abstract: This paper provides a rigorous, comprehensive assessment of the impact of mega development projects (MDPs)-defined as capital investments exceeding $1 billion in real 2015 prices-on (a) per capita real GDP growth and (b) the Human Development Index (HDI), using a calibrated synthetic project-level dataset of approximately 5,000 projects spanning 1960-2026, linked to macroeconomic panel data for 193 countries. Drawing on the conceptual and empirical framework of Amavilah (2008, 2014a, 2018); Amavilah et al. (2019); Amavilah and Andrés (2024) and the seminal megaproject literature of Flyvbjerg (2014); Ansar et al. (2014), we integrate sectoral heterogeneity, institutional quality, and geographic stratification into a unified growth model. Four principal findings emerge. First, MDPs reduce per capita growth on average-a manifestation of the "Iron Law of Megaprojects"-but produce positive Amavilah Megaprojects, Growth, and Human Development effects under sufficiently strong institutions. Second, ICT investments are consistently growth-enhancing across all income strata, while transport and dam projects exhibit high failure rates, especially in low-income and Sub-Saharan African contexts. Third, evidence is consistent with conditional β-convergence at the country level: MDPs accelerate convergence in high-institution economies yet deepen divergence elsewhere. Fourth, applying the analytical framework to Namibia's Hyphen Green Hydrogen project ($9.4-$13 billion) reveals structural characteristics-enclave export orientation, uncertain demand, thin domestic capability, and contested governancethat satisfy all necessary conditions for "white-elephanting." Policy implications for sequenced, institution-first development strategies are drawn.

title: Does Cartographic Representation Matter for Economic Performance?

detail.title: Does Cartographic Representation Matter for Economic Performance?
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether systematic distortion in global cartographic representationsspecifically the Mercator projection-has measurable and persistent economic consequences. We construct a novel GIS-based Map Distortion Index (MDI) using Natural Earth shapefiles projected under both World Mercator (EPSG:3395) and Equal Earth (EPSG:8857), defined as the log-ratio of each country's visually projected area on standard world maps relative to its true equal-area surface. We merge this country-level index with global macroeconomic panel data from the World Bank World Development Indicators (WDI, 1990-2024), Penn World Tables 10.0 (PWT), and the Maddison Project Database. We estimate whether representational distortion is associated with GDP levels, GDP per capita, and global GDP shares using a suite of empirical strategies: two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) panel regressions, difference-indifferences (DiD) with staggered adoption, event study specifications validating parallel trends, horse-race models benchmarking the MDI against population, human capital, institutional quality, and natural resource endowments, two-stage least squares (2SLS) using the analytic MDI approximation as an instrument, and a synthetic control analysis treating Sub-Saharan Africa as a composite treatment unit. Our central theoretical claim is that cartographic representation functions as an informational externality: persistent visual underrepresentation of low-latitude economies-Cartographic Distortion & Economic Performance Amavilah (2026) Africa, South America, and much of Asia-suppresses their salience in the attention sets of investors, bilateral aid donors, multinational corporations, and policymakers, with downstream consequences for capital flows, institutional prioritization, and development trajectories. We find evidence consistent with this mechanism and discuss boundary conditions, alternative explanations, and implications for representational reform.

title: Turntech: Defining an Emerging Category Through a Practitioner-Scholar Perspective on Technology-Enabled Corporate Turnaround

detail.title: Turntech: Defining an Emerging Category Through a Practitioner-Scholar Perspective on Technology-Enabled Corporate Turnaround
detail.abstract: Corporate turnaround has long remained a craft-practiced by scarce, expensive specialists, and resistant to the productization and platformization that transformed adjacent domains such as finance (fintech) and law (legaltech). This paper introduces and formally defines turntech as an emerging market category at the intersection of corporate turnaround and technology: the systematic encoding of turnaround methods into software, data, and artificial intelligence to compress the diagnosis-to-action interval, increase decision precision under distress, and democratize access to high-quality recovery for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

title: Supply Chain Collaboration as a Dynamic Operational Capability: A Multi-Method Framework of Collaborative Capabilities
affiliations: Kocaeli University,  and Kocaeli University - Engineering Faculty

detail.title: Supply Chain Collaboration as a Dynamic Operational Capability: A Multi-Method Framework of Collaborative Capabilities
detail.abstract: Supply chain cooperation (SCC) has evolved from a coordination tool to a strategic competency system. Existing information however is spread across relational, digital and resilience streams without an integrated capacity architecture with a psychometrically validated foundation. The objective of this research is to fill this gap by applying a unique four-method sequential research methodology involving Systematic Literature Review (SLR), Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) and MICMAC analysis. To our knowledge, the novel synthesis of these methodologies in the context of SCC capability building is employed for the first time. Each technique performs a separate, complementary role: SLR determines theoretical completeness, EFA offers empirical scale validation, ISM reveals hierarchical precedence links, and MICMAC classifies dimensions on the basis of their systemic driving and dependent capacities. Together they create a cohesive structural knowledge foundation from a fragmented one. Our SLR (PRISMA 2020-compliant) of 86 peer-reviewed papers (2010-2025) revealed 39 collaboration traits, organized in nine competency groups by inductive coding . The EFA results on a 35-item instrument applied to 173 supply chain experts revealed factor loadings from 0.654 to 0.913, explained variance of 74.641  and Cronbach’s alpha from 0.712 to 0.882 which validated the dimensional structure. Then the experimental hierarchical precedence of the nine dimensions was obtained using a Delphi-based ISM technique. Six of the verified dimensions were chosen as linking variables by MICMAC, Relational Capital being the structural heart of the SCC system. The combined findings support a Three-Tier SCC Capability Framework: Foundational Resources (Resource Readiness, Strategic Leadership, Organizational Alignment), Collaborative Mechanisms (Information Integration, Relational Capital, Process Integration) and Dynamic Logistics Capabilities (Digital Enablement, Adaptive Resilience, Sustainable Value Creation). Digital Enablement and Adaptive Resilience earned occupied upper hierarchical positions in the ISM model. Five study suggestions illustrate the hierarchical links between levels. The results show that digital transformation and resilience are not stand-alone achievements, but achieved through relational, organizational and leadership foundations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study integrating SLR, EFA, ISM and MICMAC into a unified SCC capability architecture, which provides a theoretically grounded framework and a validated diagnostic tool for the supply chain management research and practice.

detail.abstract: This paper builds a bridge. On the left side stands the Unified Theory of Trust-Based Decision in economics-a framework deriving structural boundaries on market concentration from demand-side cognitive constraints. On the right side stands a set of applications in computer science-AIOps fault prioritization, AI reasoning chain logical fidelity verification, and LLM lifecycle perpetual update architecture. This paper argues that these two seemingly unrelated domains share a single underlying constraint on causal transmission: signals propagating along causal edges decay at each step by an attenuation coefficient w ∈ [0,1]; signals never amplify. This constraint is formalized as three axioms of Standard Field Theory-Transmission Conservation, Compilation Conservation, and Zero-Signal Convergence. The complete transmission formulas for both homogeneous and heterogeneous scenarios are given. Impact Rate IR(v) is defined as a universal measure of intervention efficiency on causal networks. Starting from the static engine, its two boundary limitations-the requirement of a standard field environment and the assumption of one-shot intervention-naturally lead to the Dynamic Sequential Controller and the Temporal Clock, enabling sequential decision-making in nonstandard environments. This paper does not claim to have invented new mathematical tools. It argues for the existence of a previously unsystematically articulated cross-domain universal constraint.

detail.abstract: Capital-account openness can improve international risk sharing, deepen domestic financial markets, lower the cost of capital, and expand investment opportunities. Yet the same openness can also transmit global financial shocks, intensify credit booms, encourage foreign-currency leverage, amplify asset-price cycles, weaken monetary-policy autonomy, and increase the probability of currency and banking crises. This paper develops a professional, risk-governed framework for managing financial openness under crisis risk by comparing capital controls, capital-flow management measures, macroprudential policy, prudential regulation, and related policy instruments. The study synthesizes more than fifty pre-2006 foundational references on capital-account liberalization, financial repression, currency crises, sudden stops, banking fragility, speculative attacks, the impossible trinity, early-warning indicators, and the emergence of macroprudential thinking. It also connects the classic literature to recent institutional developments, including the IMF institutional view on capital flows, the operationalization of capital flow management measures and macroprudential measures, and current evidence on global financial volatility. The paper argues that capital controls and macroprudential policy should not be analyzed as ideological opposites to liberalization, but as conditional risk-management tools within a broader macro-financial policy architecture. The proposed framework distinguishes between structural vulnerabilities, cyclical pressures, crisis liquidity stress, and solvency problems; it then matches each condition with appropriate policy tools, safeguards, and exit principles. The central contribution is a comparative framework that helps emerging economies sequence financial openness while reducing crisis probability, preserving policy credibility, and avoiding the misuse of controls as substitutes for sound fiscal, monetary, institutional, and supervisory policy.

title: Caring Flexibly? Working Conditions and the Supply of Adult Care
affiliations: London School of Economics and

detail.title: Caring Flexibly? Working Conditions and the Supply of Adult Care
detail.abstract: Although flexible employment policies can help employed individuals balance caregiving and paid work, limited evidence has been devoted to examining the effect of working flexibly on the supply of care to older adults. In this paper, we study the impact of flexible working conditions on the supply of informal adult care and mental health. We exploit variation from the 2014 expansion of the Right to Request Flexible Work (RRFW) to employees in the UK. Our findings point to a gendered response to increased employment flexibility. We document a 1.3-percentage-point increase in the likelihood that men provide informal care within the household, alongside less regular daytime work, greater control over working hours, and higher engagement in home production. In contrast, among potential female caregivers, we find that the reform reduced the probability of high-intensity caregiving, which is typically incompatible with employment or related activities. We document that the increased workplace flexibility not only encourages caregiving but also helps reduce gender disparities in unpaid care. We additionally find suggestive evidence of improved mental health outcomes, particularly among men.

title: Women and the Leaky Pipeline to STEM: Is Survivorship Bias Impacting our Understanding of the Barriers to Women Leadership?

detail.title: Women and the Leaky Pipeline to STEM: Is Survivorship Bias Impacting our Understanding of the Barriers to Women Leadership?
detail.abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine the survivorship bias amongst women leaders in the technology sector. The qualitative study consisted of interviews with 15 women leaders in technology. Results suggest that 58% of women’s career obstacles relate to gender and that significant barriers such as unfair promotion opportunities and the double bind still exist. Despite this, many women leaders still believe that hard work and personality can protect against obstacles for younger women and that it is unlikely qualified future women will get passed up. Implications regarding these themes and patterns are discussed in the context of the perpetual nature of the survivorship bias from internal evaluation of the participants’ own success to external sampling and visibility issues at women in leadership speeches and events. Future directions may build on this exploratory study through longitudinal research and alternative samples of college students and individuals with intersectional identities.
