detail.title: Guarantee Companies & Development Finance: Products, Business Models & Constraints
detail.abstract:
Specialist guarantee companies can play a valuable role in financial markets when other intermediaries such as banks or bond market investors are unable or unwilling to take on specific risks. 

An example is the guarantees that monoline insurers provided for infrastructure debt in the 1990s and early 2000s. In those years, several developed-economy governments wished to raise funding for public investment without encumbering their balance sheets. Corporates also sought financing for investment purposes either through their own on-balance-sheet debt issues or via bankruptcy remote Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs). Saving institutions like pension funds lacked the infrastructure teams necessary to evaluate the complex risks involved. The solution was that monoline insurers provided guarantees, raising the ratings of bond issues. They acted as controlling creditors, monitoring project conditions and covenants on behalf of all creditors. 

The monoline insurers just described had emerged earlier in the United States (US) municipal bond market. In that context, tax considerations provided incentives that fragmented the market, motivating retail investors to invest in non-diversified ways in opaque bond issues. Again, the monolines provided a solution by supplying 100% wraps on municipal bond issues. These wraps mitigated the effects of informational asymmetry and a taxinduced lack of diversification. 

This study examines the experience of monoline insurers to see whether one may draw lessons for the use of specialist guarantee companies in Emerging Market and Developing Economy (EMDE) countries. Donor countries and Development Banks (multilateral and bilateral) have invested in specialist guarantee companies. We review the activities of these EMDE guarantee companies, commenting on constraints and the potential they offer to drive development financing. 

The report aims to inform donor-country decision makers considering whether to invest in specialist guarantee companies. We believe that in reviewing the experience of the monolines and studying EMDE guarantee companies, the study may be of interest also to operators of guarantee companies and even for institutional investors. 

Our analysis draws on interviews with more than forty industry practitioners including past and current staff of developed-market monolines, Development Finance Institutions (DFIs) and specialist EMDE guarantee funds. We analyse the financial statements and ratings of a prominent developed market monoline and two EMDE guarantee funds to understand the constraints they face, most notably the assessments they receive from rating agencies and the profitability of their business models.

title: Stripping Discount Curves Across Currencies: Transfer Learning from US Treasuries
affiliations: École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Stanford University - Department of Management Science & Engineering and Stanford

detail.title: Stripping Discount Curves Across Currencies: Transfer Learning from US Treasuries
detail.abstract: We provide precise international yield curves that constitute the new reference database for the government bond markets of six major economies, estimated with a robust and flexible machine learning method regularized by economic principles. We first show that the kernel ridge regression (KR) method of Filipovic, Pelger, and Ye (2024), the most precise method for US Treasuries, generalizes to all international bond markets and uniformly dominates the Nelson-Siegel-Svensson (NSS) benchmark used by many central banks. When foreign exchange (FX) markets provide additional information, we further improve upon KR with a novel transfer learning extension, KR-Transfer (KR-T). KR-T converts US Treasuries into target-currency "synthetic bonds" using FX spot and forward rates and estimates the discount curves jointly under a weak covered interest parity (CIP) condition, which penalizes only the curvature of the cross-currency spread and leaves its level and slope unconstrained. Under block cross-validation that mimics real-world maturity gaps, KR-T reduces out-of-sample yield errors by up to 44% relative to KR and by 68-87% relative to NSS, while matching KR where local data are sufficient. The gains concentrate at maturities where FX forwards are observed, identifying FX forward availability as the economic channel of transfer learning. KR-T also delivers more stable forward rates and more plausible yield curve dynamics.

title: Rightsizing Arbitration

detail.title: Rightsizing Arbitration

publicationDetails.detailsText: 41 Ohio St. J. on Disp. Resol. 1 (2026)

detail.abstract: Assuming the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), our country, and its democratic ideals survive 100 more years, several scenarios for its application to employment arbitration and to labor arbitration may play out. As to employment arbitration, legislators will continue to push to limit its scope, and courts will continue to develop the FAA jurisprudence in the employment area in ways that address the relatively unequal bargaining position of workers and the entities for which they labor. As to labor arbitration, courts will continue to intermittently apply the FAA without clarity as to whether it applies or is merely persuasive authority. Legislators may or may not overlook labor arbitration as they promulgate amendments and supplemental legislation to the FAA. Despite the quagmire of uncertainty about the FAA’s role in labor arbitration, development by the courts of the precise test to determine when an arbitrator exceeds their authority will continue. The system of labor arbitration and its protection of the right to strike, will be enhanced to the extent courts reconfirm that an arbitrator exceeds their authority only when they fail to interpret the collective bargaining agreement. This article first provides background for those unfamiliar with employment arbitration and labor arbitration. Second, the article explains why the use of pre-dispute arbitration of statutory employment claims is problematic and why federal legislation may or may not address this problem over the next 100 years. Third, it describes the conflict in the courts over the test for when a labor arbitrator exceeds their authority and explains the impact on collective bargaining of which interpretation prevails over the next 100 years.

title: One Axis, Two Observations: Restating the Relation between Value and Price

detail.title: One Axis, Two Observations: Restating the Relation between Value and Price
detail.abstract: In the explanation of price, value is redundant: given a system's technical and distributive conditions, prices are fully determined without appeal to value (Sraffa, 1960; Steedman, 1977). Yet value has never withdrawn; it remains in use even after being shown redundant. This paper resolves that paradox of the "redundant but indispensable." The key is to see that value and price are not two entities but two observations of a single axis — worth, the plain question "how much is this worth." Which observation one takes is fixed by function: in expressing one's own demand and closing a transaction, one looks at worth from the angle of price; in holding, for the sake of decision, a judgment aimed at the public level, one looks at worth from the angle of value. Both observe the same axis, and so do not split it but jointly reflect it. At the public level, worth has a ready objective answer — the de-biased moving centre of countless transactions, which exists yet cannot be reached exactly. A boundedly rational subject cannot reach it, and so, from local samples, estimates a reachable proxy: this is value, a cognitive proxy that compresses a diffuse price-regularity into a usable judgment. Value and price share one source and do not determine each other; the supposed "circularity of value and price" is merely the result of mistaking two observations of one axis for two entities and letting them determine each other — once the premise is exposed, it dissolves on its own. This paper is an explanatory framework. It does not claim to have explained reality, but every part of it is built to aim at reality; its legitimacy rests on parsimony, unification, and falsifiability, and it offers refutable logical prohibitions together with one directional prediction.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Portfolio Management Paradigms

detail.title: Comparative Evaluation of Portfolio Management Paradigms
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates three portfolio-management paradigms over an approximately five-year public-evidence horizon: automated robo-advisory platforms, emerging AI and machine-learning portfolio systems, and trained human managers or standard benchmark portfolios. The analysis uses risk-adjusted performance measures, observable fee schedules, official ETF and platform disclosures, academic research, and industry scorecards. Current evidence suggests that robo-advisors provide the clearest low-cost implementation case for retail investors, primarily through diversified beta exposure, automatic rebalancing, and disciplined portfolio maintenance. AI and machine-learning methods show meaningful research potential, including strong out-ofsample results in selected academic settings, but live publicly investable AI-labeled products do not yet establish broad superiority after fees, turnover, and implementation costs. Active human managers continue to face a difficult benchmark-relative performance hurdle, particularly in U.S. large-cap equities, while human advisors retain a defensible role in behavioral coaching, tax-aware planning, estate coordination, and judgment-heavy client decisions. The most plausible next-stage model is therefore not pure robo-advice, pure AI, or pure human active management, but a human-in-the-loop architecture combining automated core portfolios, AI-assisted analytics, and human oversight.

title: Rural Dengue Dynamics: The Interplay of Climate, Built Environment, and Agriculture in Costa Rica
affiliations: Stanford University, Stanford University, Stanford University, University of Costa Rica, University of Costa Rica, University of Costa Rica, , Costa Rica Ministry of Health and Stanford University

detail.title: Rural Dengue Dynamics: The Interplay of Climate, Built Environment, and Agriculture in Costa Rica
detail.abstract: Dengue is one of the world’s highest-burden arboviral diseases. Although classically considered an urban disease, many regions experience a substantial dengue burden in rural areas. The combined influence of long-term climate, short-term weather variation, local built environments, and land-use gradients on dengue dynamics in rural settings remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to predict shifting risk under global change. Here, we investigate these dynamics in Costa Rica to disentangle how these interacting socio-environmental factors shape rural dengue transmission. We first use 22 years of canton-level (admin-2) case data to establish that both dengue cases and incidence are consistently higher in rural than in urban districts. Then, using ten years of district-level (admin-3) monthly case data and a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework, we identify the climatic and land-use features most strongly associated with dengue risk. Temperature underlies broad spatial patterns in dengue’s urban–rural distribution, while precipitation effects differ between coasts, reflecting intercoastal climate zone contrasts rather than interactions between urbanization and water availability. Given suitable climate, even modest levels of built infrastructure substantially increase risk, but the relationship plateaus at higher levels of building volume. Dengue risk is also elevated in areas with high agricultural crop cover at low and mid elevations but not at higher, cooler elevations. Together these results suggest that high risk of rural dengue in Costa Rica result from climate suitability aligning with baseline levels of built infrastructure, with agriculture potentially emerging as a distinct driver of rural dengue transmission.

title: From Data Protection to Fundamental Rights: Why FRIA Represents a Significant Step Toward a Paradigm Shift in the EU AI Act

detail.title: From Data Protection to Fundamental Rights: Why FRIA Represents a Significant Step Toward a Paradigm Shift in the EU AI Act

detail.abstract: For more than a decade, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has served as the dominant paradigm for thinking about digital rights, both within the European Union and beyond. This paper employs a comparative analysis of the GDPR and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act), focusing on Article 27 of the latter, to demonstrate that the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) is not merely an extension or an upgraded version of the Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). The paper's central finding is that FRIA marks a significant, and still contested, step toward a paradigm shift from data protection to fundamental rights protection, even though many regulators and practitioners currently continue to treat it, in practice, as an extension of existing data protection assessment processes. The philosophical roots of this shift lie in the principle of human dignity as enshrined in Article 1 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. Beyond the conceptual claim, the paper also examines the economic burden that FRIA-style obligations impose, particularly on small and medium-sized enterprises and under-resourced public bodies, and situates the EU's recent decision to delay implementation within that administrative-cost context. The paper concludes that any legal system, including Iran's, currently drafting or reconsidering a governance framework for artificial intelligence, should not reduce the matter to personal data protection alone, but must instead provide independent mechanisms for fundamental rights impact assessment, algorithmic transparency, human oversight, the right to contest automated decisions, and accountability, while building proportionality to institutional capacity into the design from the outset.

detail.abstract:
Background: Early union formation (marriage or cohabitation before age 18) remains a significant public health concern in Cambodia, with wide-ranging implications for women's health, education, and economic opportunities. Educational attainment has been identified as a strong predictor of delayed marriage timing. Yet, the relationship between educational discontinuation and early union formation has not been comprehensively examined using recent nationally representative data. This study is the first to focus specifically on the Grade 9 lower secondary completion threshold using the 2021–22 CDHS, addressing an important evidence gap in the Southeast Asian literature.

Objective: To examine the association between educational discontinuation (completing fewer than 9 years of schooling) and early union formation (marriage or cohabitation before age 18) among young women in Cambodia, and to explore potential effect modification by residence and household wealth.

Methods: We analyzed data from 1,682 ever-married women aged 20–24 years from the 2021–22 Cambodia Demographic and Health Survey. Early union formation was defined as the first marriage or cohabitation before age 18. Educational discontinuation was operationalized as fewer than 9 years of schooling (i.e., not completing lower secondary education). Survey-weighted logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for residence, wealth quintile, province, and sex of the household head. Given the outcome prevalence of approximately 31%, results are presented alongside predicted probabilities and absolute risk differences to complement odds ratio estimates. Stratified analyses examined associations by urban/rural residence and household poverty status.

Results: Early union formation prevalence was 30.9% (95% CI: 27.9–33.9). Two-thirds (65.8%) of young women had discontinued education before completing lower secondary school. In fully adjusted models, educational discontinuation was strongly associated with early union formation (aOR: 2.00, 95% CI: 1.41–2.83). The predicted probability of early union formation was 35.3% among those with <9 years of schooling compared with 22.0% among those with ≥9 years, representing a 13.3 percentage-point absolute difference. Associations were observed across urban/rural strata and wealth categories, with a larger point estimate among poor households (aOR: 3.13, 95% CI: 1.74–5.61), though the interaction did not reach statistical significance (p=0.10).

Conclusions: Educational discontinuation before completing lower secondary school is robustly associated with early union formation among young Cambodian women across diverse socioeconomic contexts. These findings support policies and programs aimed at keeping girls in school through at least lower secondary completion as one component of comprehensive strategies to address early marriage in Cambodia.

detail.abstract: Long-wave scholarship has documented recurring forty-to-sixty-year economic cycles driven by infrastructure technologies but has not identified a structural mechanism that explains why every major infrastructure technology produces the same financial shape. This research note proposes that the mechanism is the simultaneous presence of industrial-scale costs that cannot be avoided and value dissolution that erodes the revenue base funding the buildout (proposed term: double bind). The note further proposes that the bind is the default trajectory of shared, privately financed infrastructure technology, and that the broad-based value creation associated with deployment phases is an engineered state requiring deliberate institutional intervention and continuous maintenance. The hypothesis draws on a sequence of seven consecutive markers identified through comparative analysis of railroads, electricity, telephony, and computing, published in the author's Silicon Industrialists series (Liberopoulou, 2026). This note states the hypothesis, identifies the published evidence base, and declares intent to develop the argument through a full literature review and working paper.

detail.abstract: The 2007-08 food price crisis is usually told as a story about weather and speculation. Rice prices rose 31 percent in a single month; wheat rose 29 percent; riots followed in more than a dozen countries. I argue in this paper that the real story sits further back, in three decades of neoliberal agricultural restructuring that had already stripped developing countries of the capacity to absorb a shock like that one. Structural adjustment programmes, trade liberalisation, and the withdrawal of state support for domestic agriculture did not simply fail to prevent the crisis of 2007-08. They built the conditions for it. Drawing on Amartya Sen's entitlement approach-the insight that hunger is a failure of access and purchasing power, not food availability-I examine two cases from that earlier period, Haiti and The Gambia, where IMF-and World Bank-mandated liberalisation left domestic rice production unable to compete with subsidised imports, deepening dependency at precisely the moment global prices spiked. I then extend the analysis to a case still unfolding as I write: Pakistan's suspension of its decades-old wheat Minimum Support Price for the 2024-25 season, followed by a hybrid, private-sector-mediated arrangement from 2025-26, both under IMF Extended Fund Facility conditionality. The policy shift has already produced sharp production declines, farmer protests, and renewed import dependency in a country that had been substantially selfsufficient in wheat. I situate this within a second global food price shock, triggered by Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and argue that the vulnerability exposed in 2007-08 was never resolved-only quietly obscured by a run of stable prices. The conclusion I drew in 2016 holds up better now than I expected it to: countries that kept domestic production capacity and negotiating leverage, India's expanding price support system chief among them, have weathered these shocks far better than countries that liberalised under outside pressure. Pakistan is the latest test of that pattern.

detail.abstract: With rising concerns about diet-related health issues and the declining quality of life due to obesity, many countries, such as the United States, have introduced taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) to decrease their consumption, improve public health, and fund health programs. A key question is whether these taxes are effective interventions, particularly for those most in need, such as individuals with hypertension, high cholesterol, type 2 diabetes, and other diet-related chronic diseases. Using the NielsenIQ Homescan Consumer Panel and Health Ailment Survey, I classify households into four health-risk subgroups via latent class analysis and apply an Augmented Synthetic Control Method across seven U.S. taxed cities, accounting for cross-border substitution. The highest-risk subgroup (High Multi-Morbidities, HMM) significantly reduces purchases, consistent with habit stock decumulation, while households with High Metabolic Dysfunction (HMD) increase purchases, reflecting continued habit stock accumulation. Low-risk households modestly reduce consumption and remain inelastic throughout. This heterogeneity in response calls for targeted interventions, such as differentiated tax rates, subsidies for healthier alternatives, and behavioral nudges to promote sustained behavioral change among vulnerable consumers.

detail.abstract: We estimate a discrete-time Markov transition model of auto loan performance over the 2000-2025 period using multinomial logistic regressions. Using rolling pseudo out-of-sample forecasts, we document persistent declines in the sensitivity of the probability of default to an unemployment shock in both the global financial crisis and Covid recessions. The estimated effect of a 1 percentage point increase in unemployment on default risk declined from 16 percent in 2006 to 3 percent post-2020. Two-year cumulative default forecasts over 2020-2021 using pre-pandemic parameters overstate actual defaults by 100 basis points (25 percent), with forecast errors largest in absolute terms for subprime borrowers and largest in relative terms for prime borrowers. The instability persists after controlling for forbearance usage and pandemic-period dummy variables, and is driven primarily by changes in macroeconomic relationships rather than borrower composition. These findings have implications for stress testing models and loss forecasting practices that rely on stable unemployment-default relationships.

title: The Impact of Committee Jurisdiction on Sell-Side Information Asymmetry

detail.title: The Impact of Committee Jurisdiction on Sell-Side Information Asymmetry

keywords: Carhart Four-Factor Model JEL Classification: G11

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether committee jurisdiction generates a detectable informational advantage in the sell-side trading behavior of members of the United States Congress following the passage of the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012. Using a rule-based committee-industry crosswalk with dynamic sessionlevel assignment, congressional stock sales are classified as jurisdictional or nonjurisdictional and evaluated through calendar-time portfolios estimated with a Carhart four-factor model. The central finding is a statistically significant short-horizon sell spread of 7.23 percent over 20 trading days, indicating that jurisdictionally relevant sales are followed by systematically more negative abnormal returns than non-jurisdictional sales. This effect is more clearly differentiated in the House of Representatives, consistent with the narrower and more specialized committee structure of that chamber. Committee-level evidence is more exploratory and should be interpreted with caution. The results do not constitute evidence of unlawful insider trading but suggest that the deterrent effect of the STOCK Act may be incomplete and localized, concentrated within specific institutional channels rather than distributed across the legislative branch as a whole.

title: Khan | New Public Management and Privatisation in Pakistan: Promise, Performance, and the Path Forward

detail.title: Khan | New Public Management and Privatisation in Pakistan: Promise, Performance, and the Path Forward
detail.abstract: New Public Management (NPM) emerged in the 1980s as the dominant international paradigm for reforming state institutions, promising greater efficiency, accountability, and responsiveness through market mechanisms, competitive tendering, performance measurement, and disaggregation of public bureaucracies. Pakistan adopted key elements of this agenda-most consequentially through its privatisation programme launched in 1991-under sustained pressure from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank as conditions of structural adjustment lending. This paper assesses the three-decade record of NPM-informed reform in Pakistan, with particular attention to the privatisation of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) across banking, energy, fertiliser, and industrial sectors. Drawing on empirical evidence from Pakistan and international comparative literature, and updated to reflect Pakistan's current SOE reform agenda under the 2024 IMF Extended Fund Facility, the paper argues that Pakistan's privatisation experience demonstrates the critical importance of three preconditions that NPM theory assumes but Pakistan rarely provided: transparent process, competitive post-privatisation markets, and governance capacity in regulatory institutions. Where these preconditions were absent, privatisation transferred inefficiency from public to private hands rather than eliminating it. The paper concludes that Pakistan's renewed privatisation push under the 2024-26 IMF programme faces the same structural constraints unless regulatory reform and governance strengthening accompany divestment.

The Abbottabad Sustainable Strategy for Development, which this paper examines, was itself facilitated by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) with partial international donor funding; the author's analysis of that strategy was undertaken independently and was not commissioned or funded by IUCN or any other party involved in the ASSD's original design or implementation.

detail.abstract: Pakistan is urbanising faster than any other country in South Asia. Roughly 38 percent of its population already lives in cities, a share that has climbed steadily and will keep climbing. 1 Yet the governance of those cities remains structurally fragmented: responsibilities split between federal, provincial, and local tiers, revenue authority sitting above while service obligations sit below, and participation that is either absent or largely ceremonial. I examine the Abbottabad Sustainable Strategy for Development (ASSD) here-a multisectoral urban governance initiative built for Abbottabad, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's third-largest city, in 2004-as a case study of what post-devolution urban governance in Pakistan attempted, what it actually delivered, and where it fell short. Drawing on Pierre's framework of urban governance modes, Arnstein's (1969) ladder of citizen participation, and Blanco's (2013) networked governance model, I argue that the ASSD was a genuine, if ultimately incomplete, experiment in participatory urban planning-and that its partial failures say something real about the structural constraints still limiting urban governance across Pakistan two decades later. I close by situating Abbottabad's experience within the Asian Development Bank's 2024 national urban assessment, which finds that Pakistan's urban governance challenges have deepened, not resolved, in the years since.

title: From Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment to a Cognitive Transparency Requirement: A Blueprint for the Third Generation of AI Governance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment to a Cognitive Transparency Requirement: A Blueprint for the Third Generation of AI Governance
detail.abstract: AI governance has so far centered on two pillars: personal data protection and fundamental rights. Drawing on recent empirical evidence-including the BCG Henderson Institute report and Lee et al. (2025, CHI)-this paper argues that a third generation of AI governance must address a phenomenon absent from existing frameworks such as Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) and Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIA): organization-wide distributed deskilling. The paper first shows why the competing approach-a "Cognitive Impact Assessment" premised on directly measuring users' minds-fails on grounds of evidentiary burden, causal attribution, epistemic paternalism, and scalability. It then proposes an alternative framework, the "Cognitive Transparency Requirement," which shifts the locus of assessment from the user's mind to the system's observable behavior, operationalized through an "Effective Human Oversight Rate" (EHOR) metric. The paper closes with design safeguards against performative compliance and responses to anticipated objections-including the flawed calculator analogy and concerns over regulatory burden-culminating in a proposal for integration into Article 6 of the EU AI Act.

title: Concurrent Wasting and Stunting Among Children in Mozambique: Determinants and Predicted Burden Under Nutrition and WASH Scenarios
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Concurrent Wasting and Stunting Among Children in Mozambique: Determinants and Predicted Burden Under Nutrition and WASH Scenarios
detail.abstract: Background: Concurrent wasting and stunting (WaSt) identifies children with compounded anthropometric deficits, but evidence on determinants and predicted burden is limited in climate-shock prone settings like Mozambique. This study examined WaSt correlates and predicted burden under plausible improvements in diet, breastfeeding, and WASH.Methods: Quantitative cross-sectional surveys of children aged 0–59 were analysed. Logistic models estimated unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios between determinants and WaSt, and compared results with wasting and stunting. A predictive model simulated WaSt reduction given improvements in minimum dietary diversity, exclusive breastfeeding, and basic water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH).Results: The sample included 20,148 children. WaSt prevalence averaged 2.05%. In the fully adjusted model, WaSt was more strongly associated with age 12–23 months, diarrhoea, fever, lower wealth, lower caregiver education, and absence of basic sanitation. WaSt shared determinants with both wasting and stunting but had a sharper morbidity and sanitation profile. Climate markers were not clearly associated with WaSt after adjustment. The simulated scenario including all improvements reduced predicted prevalence from 2.06% to 1.11%.Conclusions: WaSt clustered around early childhood, morbidity, sanitation, and socioeconomic disadvantage. The analysis of climate risk showed no increased prevalence in high-risk settings. Scenario modelling suggests that integrated diet, breastfeeding, and WASH improvements could lower predicted burden. Taken together, these findings provide relevant insights on WaSt and the relevance of integrated nutrition programming to address its determinants.

title: Antibiotic Use in Community Pharmacies Across Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

detail.title: Antibiotic Use in Community Pharmacies Across Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests

detail.abstract:
Background: Dispensing of antibiotics without prescription is common in community pharmacies and drug outlets (CPDOs) in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and is likely to contribute to the high regional burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet comprehensive evidence on the extent of this practice remains limited. This review aimed to quantify the prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic dispensing in CPDOs across SSA.

Methods: Scholarly databases up to April 2025 were systematically searched for empirical studies examining non-prescription antibiotic dispensing in CPDOs in SSA. Observational, mixed-methods, and randomized controlled studies conducted and published between 2015 and 2025 were eligible. Study quality was assessed using the CASP Cross-Sectional Studies checklist. Data on dispensing practices were analyzed using proportional meta-analysis with a random-effects model in R. The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF ID: 10.17605/OSF.IO/YDTA2).

Results: Eighteen studies involving 2,298 CPDOs across eight SSA countries were included. The pooled prevalence of non-prescription antibiotic dispensing was 68% (95% CI: 63%–72%). Antibiotics were commonly dispensed without prescription for upper respiratory tract infections (45% encounters, 95% CI: 40%–50%) and acute diarrhea (36% encounters, 95% CI: 30%–43%). According to the WHO AWaRe classification, 36% of dispensed antibiotics were from the Access category, 22% from the Watch category, and 2% from the Reserve category.

Conclusion: Non-prescription antibiotic dispensing in CPDOs is widespread in SSA, frequently for self-limiting conditions. Integrating CPDOs into innovative national antimicrobial stewardship programs is necessary to address AMR in the region.

detail.abstract: The paper examines the compatibility of licensing negotiation groups (LNGs) with Article 101 TFEU in the context of standard essential patent (SEP) licensing. While LNGs have been proposed as a mechanism to improve efficiency in licensing negotiations, their introduction raises important competition law questions. The analysis considers the framework set out in the European Commission's revised Technology Transfer Guidelines and explores how it applies to the specific characteristics of SEP licensing. In particular, it highlights challenges related to market definition and the assessment of buyer power. The paper further discusses the conditions under which LNGs may generate efficiencies and deliver benefits to consumers. Against this background, it identifies areas where further clarification and empirical evidence may be needed to ensure a consistent and balanced application of competition law.

detail.abstract: A team in a round-robin group whose own qualification is already settled (clinched or eliminated) can still determine which other teams advance; we call this residual sovereignty. We show that this is a pure size phenomenon. For any admissible ranking rule (monotone, neutral, efficient, robust to tiebreakers), a group admits no robust kingmaker if and only if n ≤ 3; for additive scoring rules the same threshold holds exactly, independent of the number of qualifiers m and the win value. Second, we show pricing cannot even limit their impact: under any fixed tiebreaker, the worst-case total "reach" of kingmakers is a closed-form function of (n, m) only, identical for all win values and maximized by a structural balance around ⌊n 2 /4⌋. Hence scoring rules cannot remove or meaningfully contain residual sovereignty. Combining this with Vong (2017), the only format eliminating both own-progress manipulation and residual sovereignty is top-one qualification from groups of at most three teams.

title: Does Stronger Supplier-Customer Relationship Reduce Trade Credit Default?
affiliations: Oklahoma State University - Stillwater - Department of Finance and Independent

detail.title: Does Stronger Supplier-Customer Relationship Reduce Trade Credit Default?
detail.abstract: We examine whether the intensity of supplier-customer relationships reduces trade credit bad debt. Using 24,145 U.S. firm-year observations from 2001 to 2024, we measure relationship intensity as the share of disclosed segment revenues directed toward identifiable named corporate counterparties (named share). Stronger relationships significantly reduce next-year bad debt (β =-0.078, t =-3.29), robust to two-digit SIC industry and year fixed effects, four alternative variable constructions, two-way clustering, and a control function test that formally rejects endogeneity (Hausman F = 0.33, p = 0.569). The coefficient strengthens to-0.105 after controlling for operational efficiency, confirming the baseline is conservative. Two channels govern cross-sectional heterogeneity: a bargaining power channel, in which the screening benefit weakens as customer-base concentration rises; and a reputation-based learning channel, in which the effect is statistically zero for young firms and grows monotonically to-0.175 for firms aged 24 years (t =-6.23). R&D intensity independently predicts lower bad debt (β =-0.203, t =-3.36), linking innovation-oriented customer ties to higher credit quality through a channel distinct from named share. Leads tests and placebo regressions confirm the result is specific to the credit screening channel. Our findings are based on mandatory SFAS 131 disclosures of U.S. public firms, which capture only customers exceeding 10% of revenues; the true effect of relationship intensity may be understated for firms with many moderate-sized named customers.

title: Lender-Borrower Interactions and Loan Contracting
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology - Department of Accounting, University of Southern California and University of California, Davis

detail.title: Lender-Borrower Interactions and Loan Contracting
detail.abstract: In commercial lending, lenders interact with borrowers to source new loans and assess credit risk. Using proprietary data from a bank, we study what drives lender-borrower interactions and how they shape loan contracting. Interactions increase with borrowers' business prospects and risks, consistent with prospecting and credit assessment motives. Although interaction-derived information is not incorporated into the bank's internal risk ratings, loans initiated after interactions are priced more efficiently, with interest rates that better predict future defaults, especially when interactions are more likely to generate new information. Loan officers use interaction-derived information to approve loans that would otherwise be rejected, but not to reject loans that would otherwise be approved; this asymmetry is more pronounced when their prospecting incentives are stronger. These findings highlight how loan officers collect and use interaction-derived information with their prospecting and screening incentives and have implications for research on loan officer incentives and the role of information in credit decisions.

title: The Law of Employee Distillation and Cloning
affiliations: School of Law, City University of Hong Kong

detail.title: The Law of Employee Distillation and Cloning
detail.abstract:
The next generation of workplace AI may not merely replace employees; it may be trained to become them. Employers can now feed an employee’s emails, chats, documents, meeting transcripts, code reviews, and behavioral traces into AI systems that reproduce not simply discrete outputs, but working style, tacit judgment, institutional memory, and professional persona. This Article calls this practice employee distillation and cloning, and offers the first systematic legal account of this emerging practice that marks a new frontier in the propertization of labor. 

Existing law appears, at first glance, to offer employees many possible avenues of protection: privacy and data protection law, copyright, trade secret law’s general skill, knowledge, and experience doctrine, the right of publicity, and contract law. Yet these protections largely dissolve upon closer inspection. Privacy law regulates only narrow forms of intrusive collection; data protection remains fragmented and uneven; copyright and trade secret laws often favor employers; right of publicity doctrine rarely reaches ordinary working identity; and contract law converts structural inequality into formal consent. The result, as this Article terms it, is a “rights mirage”: the appearance of legal protection without meaningful control.

This Article further argues that the mirage matters. Although unregulated distillation may generate short-term productivity gains, it may also impose costs that firms do not fully internalize. These costs include productivity losses and organizational friction resulting from employee resistance, degraded knowledge sharing, reduced human-capital investment, impaired mobility, weakened cumulative innovation, and distinct dignitary and autonomy harms. The Article therefore calls for future governance directed not at prohibiting employee distillation, but at structuring it through notice, meaningful consent or bargaining, use limits, compensation, and collective governance.

title: When Cost Discipline Becomes Self-Harm: A Margin-Based Early Indicator of Over-Optimisation in U.S. Retail
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: When Cost Discipline Becomes Self-Harm: A Margin-Based Early Indicator of Over-Optimisation in U.S. Retail
detail.abstract:
ABSTRACT

In this research, we test for the existence of an optimal degree of cost optimization in the context of US retailing in view of the well known focus on SG&A (Selling, general and administrative expenses) optimization and maximizing the gross margin for creating shareholder value. We pose the question of whether the excessive cost optimization is actually harmful in such a manner that it happens before the actual revenue drop is seen. In order to test our hypotheses, we use an annual panel of 13 large US retailers during the years 2004 - 2025 with two-way fixed effects regressions, a composite index approach, and a specially developed classifier. Our results come in three parts. Firstly, SG&A expenses in retailing react to revenue symmetrically; therefore, over-optimization occurs not through under-costing but through constant optimization that cannot be controlled by traditional methods. Secondly, the increase in gross margin predicts the reduction in revenue growth as well as customer satisfaction next year. What is interesting, the same measure predicts two different independent results under wild cluster bootstrap correction due to low number of clusters which we interpret as quality deterioration caused by profit-maximization in supplier margins. Thirdly, we develop a classifier based on financial measures that can predict next-year revenue losses with AUC of 0.70.

Keywords: retail operations; cost optimization; gross margin; customer satisfaction; panel data; early-warning classification.

title: U.S. Risk and Treasury Convenience
affiliations: University of California, Davis, Bank of England, European University Institute and Bank of England

detail.title: U.S. Risk and Treasury Convenience
detail.abstract: We document a rise in investors' assessment of U.S. risk relative to other G.7 economies since the late 1990s, driven by higher permanent risk but not reflected in currency returns. We investigate these facts using a two-country, incomplete-markets framework with trade in risky assets, currencies, and a rich maturity structure of bonds that earn convenience yields. Based on this, we estimate an equilibrium relationship among relative country risk, crossborder convenience yields, and carry-trade returns. We show that rising relative permanent risk explains about 62% and 47% of the decline in long-maturity convenience yields over 2002-2006 and 2010-2014, respectively.

title: From Information Abundance to Clarity Scarcity: Informational Architecture, Market Governance, and Digital Competition
affiliations: University of Southampton

detail.title: From Information Abundance to Clarity Scarcity: Informational Architecture, Market Governance, and Digital Competition
detail.abstract: Digital markets are characterized by unprecedented informational abundance, yet consumers frequently experience confusion arising from similarity among offerings, informational overload, and ambiguity in claims. We conceptualize these conditions as manifestations of a broader problem of informational architecture and develop a microeconomic framework in which market performance depends on the clarity of the informational environment. Clarity is modeled as a structural parameter capturing the extent to which consumers can identify, interpret, and evaluate relevant information when making decisions. The model demonstrates that improvements in clarity increase market participation and consumer welfare by reducing search frictions, interpretive costs, and informational asymmetries. Clarity also strengthens firms' incentives to invest in differentiation and quality enhancement, generating welfare gains through both demand-side and supply-side channels. In addition, the framework connects informational architecture to the demand-rotation literature by showing that clarity affects both the mean and dispersion of consumer valuations, thereby influencing equilibrium pricing through demand-shift and demand-rotation mechanisms. While greater clarity generally increases total surplus, surplus extraction by platforms and producers generates an efficiencydistribution trade-off, while governance costs produce an interior optimum in transparency and informational oversight. The analysis contributes to the literatures on information economics, obfuscation, market design, and platform governance by formalizing clarity as a market-wide determinant of participation, pricing, differentiation, surplus allocation, and welfare. More fundamentally, the paper argues that informational architecture is emerging as a core institution of digital markets. Just as property rights, disclosure systems, and contract enforcement shape exchange in traditional markets, algorithmically governed informational architectures increasingly determine how information becomes visible, comparable, credible, and actionable, thereby shaping the conditions under which competition, exchange, and value creation occur.

title: The Judge Lottery: Within-Office Disparities in Social Security Disability Adjudication, Fiscal Year 2025

detail.title: The Judge Lottery: Within-Office Disparities in Social Security Disability Adjudication, Fiscal Year 2025

detail.abstract: A claimant who appeals a denied Social Security disability claim is assigned, essentially at random, to an administrative law judge (ALJ) within a hearing office. Using the Social Security Administration's public ALJ disposition files for fiscal year 2025, I measure how much that assignment matters. Among 1,023 judges who issued at least 100 decisions in a single office (317,462 decisions in total), allowance rates ranged from 8.8 percent to 92.8 percent. The disparity is not primarily geographic: 73 percent of the variance in judge allowance rates lies within hearing offices rather than between them, and in the median office the gap between the most and least generous judge is 32.6 percentage points. A simulation in which every judge in an office decides identical case pools shows that sampling noise can account for only about 5 percent of the observed within-office variance. Judge allowance rates are also highly stable across years (r = 0.93 between FY2025 and FY2026 year-to-date), which rules out one-off docket composition as an explanation. Office-level workload measures (average processing time, backlog per disposition) explain little of either the level or the spread of allowance rates, and a state-month panel of initial-level determinations from 2015 to 2026 shows only a small association between backlog pressure and allowance rates. The judge draw remains one of the largest observable determinants of whether a disability appeal succeeds, a decade after the agency's quality-review reforms.

title: Public Debt Bubbles and Maturity Management

detail.title: Public Debt Bubbles and Maturity Management
detail.abstract: Public debt can retain value relative to aggregate output without giving the treasury usable financing in every state. This paper separates long-run valuation from the implementation problem created by a finite menu of maturities in a stochastic overlapping generations economy. The government intertemporal budget yields a valuation criterion that accounts for population and output growth and reduces to the interest-growth comparison in the deterministic case. At equilibrium prices, resale gains on finitely many non-contingent bonds can span state-contingent rollover revenue when signed positions are allowed. Requiring non-negative issuance instead confines feasible plans to a convex cone and yields a dual test for exclusion. Because household consumption and bond prices respond to policy, the cone is endogenous. Changes in transfer incidence, growth dispersion, persistence, and risk aversion can shift the cone as well as change its width. Persistence can improve long-run valuation while ruling out a target financing direction, and changes in household allocation can offset or reverse the price effect calculated with consumption held fixed. Very long maturities add little flexibility because their rollover payoffs approach a common direction.

title: Cliff Cuts and Equilibrium Regimes: Identification from a Cross-Chain Decentralized-Lending Reform
affiliations: Royal Institute of Technology (KTH)

detail.title: Cliff Cuts and Equilibrium Regimes: Identification from a Cross-Chain Decentralized-Lending Reform
detail.abstract: How does a reform that changes the slope of a governance-set pricing rule move its equilibrium? Decentralized lending protocols clear borrow rates through a kinked schedule, gentle below a target utilization and steep above it, the same two-slope structure that prices bank reserves, deposit-insurance premia, and capital surcharges. We exploit Aave Payload 216, a December 2024 reform that raised the below-kink slope on every stablecoin pool while cutting the above-kink cliff slope on only a subset, and difference out the common raise to identify the cut on an eight-pool on-chain panel. Treated pools migrate from the above-kink to the belowkink regime, their probability of above-kink operation falling by about 73 percentage points and staying low, a transition that holds against a clean external control of untreated Compound and SparkLend pools, persists for six months, and recurs out of sample on Aave's Polygon pools. Modeling utilization as a slope-restored mean-reverting process, we recover a cliff-discipline coefficient that scales restoration to the rate-function slope with close to unit elasticity and bounds the borrower's demand semi-elasticity at the kink. Rate dispersion compresses by 74 to 99 percent on every treated pool, while a single uncut steep-cliff pool instead shows variance expansion. The cleared rate also falls, a bounded secondary effect.

detail.abstract: The constitutional viability of reparations for Black Americans remains unresolved while opponents weaponize it to forestall legislative action. This Article argues that a well-designed reparations program targeting Black Americans harmed by documented federal housing discrimination is constitutionally sound. Drawing on the Thirteenth Amendment’s Section 2 enforcement power, the Fourteenth Amendment’s Section 5 remedial authority, and Congress’s Spending Clause privileges; this Article constructs an affirmative constitutional foundation for reparations. It then confronts Equal Protection, the primary constitutional challenge. This Article argues that the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Students for Fair Admissions presents a far narrower obstacle than critics assume. A reparations program grounded in the documented record of federal housing discrimination is legally distinguishable from programs the Court has struck down. Remediation of identified governmental wrongs is not the same as prospective racial preference, and existing doctrine preserves meaningful space for the former. This Article proposes a program design framework that maximizes constitutional durability while delivering substantive relief.

detail.abstract: We develop a parsimonious discrete-time open-economy monetary model with partial dollarization, sticky prices, an endogenous and persistent exchange-rate risk premium, and endogenous money supply, and use it to ask how dollarization shapes a small open economy's exposure to external monetary shocks. We microfound the money-demand and uncovered-parity blocks from household optimization, and a single dollarization wedge enters the reduced form through a closed-form coefficient that depends only on the steady-state dollarization share, which keeps the channel analytically transparent. We calibrate the model to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a leading high-dollarization economy, and derive closed-form comparative statics that we verify numerically and over five thousand random calibrations. A money-supply shock generates a persistent depreciation and inflation that dollarization amplifies by weakening real money demand. The transmission of foreign shocks runs through two channels. Under the bare uncovered-parity channel, a U.S. tightening raises inflation pass-through, in proportion to the interest semi-elasticity, while leaving the exchange rate close to unchanged; this exact invariance isolates where dollarization does not operate. Once the premium loads on the global rate through dollarized balance sheets, as the positive global-rate loading we estimate suggests, the same tightening produces a capital-flight depreciation that is larger the more dollarized the economy. Dollarization therefore amplifies external monetary shocks through the steady state, the inflation pass-through, and a balance-sheet exchange-rate channel.

detail.abstract:
This final report examines the January 2026 Venezuela oil operation as a case study in resource governance, executive discretion, sanctions administration, and public-accountability failure. Drawing on public reporting, court records, enforcement materials, congressional correspondence, market data, and government statements, the report assembles a chain of events that has often been reported in fragments but rarely analyzed as a single governance structure. 
The analysis begins with a market fact that narrows the question: the United States did not need Venezuelan oil in the aggregate, but specific refineries, traders, asset holders, and politically connected intermediaries stood to benefit from renewed access to Venezuelan heavy sour crude. It then traces the relationship among the Citgo acquisition by Paul Singer's Elliott-backed Amber Energy, the restoration of Venezuelan crude flows, exclusive or early oil-trading roles assigned to Vitol and Trafigura, the use of Qatar and later U.S.-controlled accounts for oil proceeds, the involvement of sanctioned Venezuelan officials, and the emergence of a Washington lobbying market around access to Venezuelan oil and natural resources.
The report's central contribution is the "missing ledger" framework. Oversight cannot begin only with the bank account into which proceeds were deposited. It must begin at the barrel: who measured the oil, who priced it, who approved discounts and fees, who captured trading margins, and how the resulting proceeds were reconciled before reaching U.S.-controlled accounts. Without a transparent barrel-to-dollar audit trail, neither Congress nor the Venezuelan public can determine whether the oil was sold at fair value or whether politically connected intermediaries captured value upstream. 
The report does not allege criminal conduct by any named individual or company. Rather, it identifies a pattern of opaque decision-making involving foreign oil assets, confidential licenses, revenue custody, sanctions discretion, creditor displacement, private lobbying, war-powers avoidance, and congressional non-action. It concludes that the Venezuela operation warrants formal oversight, including disclosure of license terms, pricing formulas, revenue-account structures, audit mechanisms, conflict reviews, and communications between U.S. officials and private beneficiaries.

title: Noise-Cancelling Location Models

detail.title: Noise-Cancelling Location Models
detail.abstract: We introduce a novel class of observation-driven location models featuring a filtering mechanism that selectively discards incoming information when it is deemed uninformative. Specifically, the proposed filter attenuates the influence of the forcing variable whenever the absolute one-step-ahead prediction error falls below a threshold, thereby mitigating the impact of noise. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator for the static parameters under both correct model specification and misspecification. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical relevance of the proposed noise-cancelling filter through empirical applications to the U.S. unemployment rate and the U.S. PCE inflation rate. The results indicate that the new approach can yield improvements in both in-sample fit and outof-sample forecasting performance relative to standard observation-driven models.

detail.title: The Interplay between Investment and Input-Output Networks in Monetary Transmission
detail.abstract: This paper examines how investment and input-output networks interact in transmitting U.S. monetary policy shocks to sectoral stock returns. We develop a theoretical multisector model featuring an adjusted-investment network, capturing investment-linkage transmission amplified by input-output linkages. Using a heterogeneous panel spatial autoregressive model with orthogonalized monetary policy shocks, we find that the adjusted-investment network accounts for 38% of the total stock-return response. Moreover, indirect spillovers through adjusted-investment linkages account for 33% of the total effect, comparable to 41% through input-output linkages. Therefore, the interplay between the two networks is an important channel of monetary transmission.

title: Does Disclosure of Shadow Bank Exposures Affect Bank Risk Management?

detail.title: Does Disclosure of Shadow Bank Exposures Affect Bank Risk Management?
detail.abstract: This study examines whether disclosure regulation affects banks' risk management. In May 2024, U.S. regulators mandated enhanced disclosure of lending to shadow banks to facilitate monitoring of the loan risk. Using a difference-indifferences design, we find that affected banks strengthen risk oversight by increasing hiring in regulatory compliance, audit, and information technology. The enhanced risk management is concentrated among banks with greater shadow bank exposure, higher ex ante credit risk, and stronger incentives to demonstrate high quality of loans extended to shadow banks in public disclosures. We further document evidence suggesting positive spillover effects to shadow banks: nonbank mortgage lenders reduce risky loan origination and experience a significant decline in consumer complaints. Collectively, our findings indicate that disclosure regulation influences banks' risk management practices by inducing them to internalize the risks arising from their partnerships with shadow banks.

title: When Markets Fail in Plain Sight: Analyst Consensus, Institutional Constraints, and Predictable Mispricings in the S&P 500

detail.title: When Markets Fail in Plain Sight: Analyst Consensus, Institutional Constraints, and Predictable Mispricings in the S&P 500
detail.abstract: In October 2022, Meta Platforms traded at $93 per share while the consensus analyst price target stood at $155 — a 67% implied upside disseminated daily in public research. Quasi-indexer institutions held approximately 76% of the float. The price declined for another six weeks before more than doubling over the subsequent twelve months. We document that this episode represents a systematic pattern. Using 21,846 S&P 500 ticker-quarters from 2010 to 2024, we show that the joint condition of unusually high analyst consensus upside (top decile of a firm's own history) and high quasi-indexer ownership predicts 6-month forward returns with a factor-adjusted alpha of 949 basis points per year (t = 3.40; non-parametric placebo p = 0.032 at 500 iterations). Neither variable alone predicts returns: upside alone yields alpha = 306 bps (t = 0.76); quasi-indexer ownership alone alpha = 77 bps (t = 0.40) — classic moderator evidence. The effect is concentrated in the post-2017 regime (alpha = 1,090 bps, t = 2.72) and absent in 2010–2016 (alpha = −319 bps). Rolling five-year windows corroborate the break, with the sign flip occurring as aggregate quasi-indexer ownership crosses approximately 0.78 — the level at which constrained capital becomes the dominant marginal price-setter. The S&P 500 appears informationally efficient (professional analysts correctly identify cross-sectional discounts in real time) but structurally inefficient: the capital that observes these discounts is bound by benchmark mandates that prohibit exploiting them. Family offices, endowments, and individuals without such mandates can implement the strategy using entirely public data.

title: Monetary Policy Regime Persistence and Equity Market Dynamics in India: A Markov-Switching Monte Carlo Framework

detail.title: Monetary Policy Regime Persistence and Equity Market Dynamics in India: A Markov-Switching Monte Carlo Framework
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between the stance of Indian monetary policy and the distribution of equity returns, and asks a deliberately modest question: not whether interest-rate policy predicts the market, but whether the persistence of policy regimes can be exploited to characterise the uncertainty surrounding future returns. Using monthly observations on the Reserve Bank of India’s repo rate and the Nifty 50 index over the period 2010 to 2025, each month has been classified into one of three policy regimes—easing, neutral, or tightening—according to the deviation of the prevailing rate from its twelve-month rolling average. The evolution of these regimes is modelled as a first-order, time-homogeneous Markov chain, and the chain is coupled to regime-conditional return distributions through a Monte Carlo simulation that generates a probability distribution over future index paths. The estimated transition matrix is strongly diagonal: every self-transition probability exceeds 0.90, and direct transitions between the easing and tightening states are never observed, the neutral state serving as an obligatory intermediate phase. A likelihood-ratio test of homogeneity (LR = 2.846, p = 0.828) does not reject the assumption that the transition matrix is stable across sub-periods. Out-of-sample, with all parameters estimated on data through 2022 and the model run forward into a 2023–2025 holdout, the realised index remains within the ninety-per-cent prediction band for the entire thirty-six-month window. The framework is not offered as a point predictor but as an instrument of policy-conditioned risk assessment. Its regime conditional returns are drawn from heavy-tailed Student-t distributions calibrated to the pronounced excess kurtosis the data exhibit, so that the resulting prediction intervals reflect the asymmetric crash risk a Gaussian specification understates. The framework’s contribution lies in furnishing a transparent, policy-conditioned account of the dispersion of outcomes rather than a single fragile point. Analysis of variance across regimes finds no statistically significant difference in mean returns, a result that is itself instructive: the influence of the policy cycle on Indian equities is visible in the shape of the return distribution far more than in its centre.

detail.abstract:
Fundamentals of Capital Taxation is the fifth book in the Fundamentals of Taxation series. It completes the series’ coverage of the tax base, after the volumes on (personal and corporate) income taxes and indirect taxes. This volume stands as a comprehensive primer on the legal and policy dimensions of capital taxation, offering readers a clear and accessible entry point into one of the most complex and debated areas of contemporary tax law.

The book opens with a substantive introduction that situates capital taxation within its historical, policy and legal context. It then proceeds to the core chapters, which are dedicated to the main forms of capital taxation: taxes on capital ownership (net wealth taxes, real estate taxes and others), capital transfers (estate, inheritance and gift taxes, financial transaction taxes, stamp duties and real estate transfer taxes), and capital gains. Further chapters explore the treatment of capital in tax treaties and address the issues of capital tax planning and avoidance.

Throughout, the volume underscores the multiplicity and fragmentation of capital taxes across jurisdictions, highlighting the legal, practical and policy challenges that arise from their lack of coordination. It emphasizes the importance of understanding the interplay between different capital taxes and their relationship with income and consumption taxes.

The book is conceived as a guide for students, academics and experienced professionals alike. It aims to provide conceptual clarity for anyone seeking a broad and nuanced understanding of capital taxation and its role in shaping fair and efficient tax systems.

detail.title: SEI: A Synthetic Euro Index for Eurozone Sovereign Debt Stabilization A Rule-Based Instrument for Generating Structural Demand Across Eurozone Sovereign Bonds
detail.abstract: We propose the Synthetic Euro Index (SEI), a rule-based nancial instrument representing a dynamic basket of all Eurozone sovereign bonds. Unlike previous proposals such as Eurobonds or Sovereign Bond-Backed Securities (SBBS/ESBies), SEI does not replace national debt issuance nor requires tranching. Instead, it operates as an additional layer generating structural demand for the underlying sovereigns, with portfolio weights determined by an algorithmic function primarily driven by GDP shares. We formalize the instrument's composition function, derive equilibrium conditions showing how SEI compresses sovereign spreads proportionally to its market size, and identify a virtuous feedback loop whereby GDP-weighted demand lowers borrowing costs, stimulating growth, which in turn increases the country's weight. A historical simulation over the period 20102024 demonstrates that a SEI of moderate size (515% of aggregate outstanding debt) would have signicantly reduced peripheral spreads during the sovereign debt crisis without eliminating market discipline.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Three-Trap Economy framework to explain why Kenya's manufacturing sector contracted, formal employment declined, and private sector credit stagnated despite ten consecutive central bank rate cuts between August 2024 and February 2026. The framework identifies three structural conditions that interact to suppress monetary policy transmission and productive investment: first, the Monetary Policy Blind Spot, in which commercial banks cannot assess the creditworthiness of informal sector borrowers and therefore cannot transmit central bank rate signals to 84% of Kenya's employed population; second, the Formality Penalty, the aggregate cost disadvantage borne by formal businesses relative to informal competitors and imports that makes formal manufacturing structurally uncompetitive; and third, the Legibility Loop, a self-reinforcing condition in which the benefits of formalization are deferred behind compliance cost thresholds that the businesses most in need of formal credit cannot afford to cross. The paper draws on data from the Central Bank of Kenya, the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics, the Kenya Association of Manufacturers, and published bank earnings reports to show that these three conditions generate a doom loop: government borrowing crowds out private credit, manufacturing declines, formal employment falls, the tax base narrows, and the government borrows more. The paper introduces the concept of the effective monetary policy transmission rate as a measurable policy variable and argues that building formal legibility infrastructure for the informal sector is the highest-priority intervention available for simultaneously addressing the credit market failure, the manufacturing decline, and the fiscal constraint. Implications for the Central Bank of Kenya, the National Treasury, and financial sector regulators are discussed.

detail.abstract: This paper studies when economic claims are meaningful. I develop a framework that treats economic models as a language and distinguishes three objects: syntax, which defines admissible economic statements; semantics, which gives those statements truth conditions by linking assumptions to observables; and pragmatics, which governs their use in prediction, communication, and policy analysis. The framework unifies several domains that are often studied separately. In identification and structural inference, it shows how causal and counterfactual claims acquire content only through explicit assumptions. In communication and information design, it clarifies how the informational environment constrains what prices, signals, and messages can convey. In welfare analysis and social choice, it characterizes normative claims as requiring an additional translation from model primitives to evaluative criteria. The paper derives a semantic ledger that records the assumptions needed to interpret positive, counterfactual, and welfare statements and thereby makes precise what an economic claim does, and does not, mean.

detail.abstract: We explored relationships between demographic variables and organizational commitment in a sample of fractionally employed C-Suite executives. In addition, we attempted to ascertain the effects that demographic variables may have on executives' protean and boundaryless career orientations. Survey data from 170 fractional executives across diverse industries was used to assess the effects of age, gender, tenure, education, role and industry on executives' commitment and career orientation. Six regression models yielded mixed results suggesting that only tenure and education emerge as significant predictors of overall commitment. A closer look at the three components of commitment suggested that age is the sole predictor of affective commitment; likewise, age and tenure emerge as predictors of normative commitment; education emerged as a predictor of continuance commitment. And while age appears to be the sole predictor of boundaryless attitudes, no demographic variable emerged as predictor of protean attitudes. Analysis of Variance suggested a statistically significant difference in commitment level across executive C-Suite roles and across industry sectors. Overall, the amount of variance in commitment explained by age, gender, tenure and education is negligible with R 2 values ranging from two percent to a high seven percent, and with seven out of 24 regression coefficients emerging as statistically significant across our six regression models. Thus, the explanatory power of the regression models appears relatively limited, suggesting that demographic variables may possess inherently low explanatory capacity within modern flexible work arrangements.

title: The Unpriced Value of Time: A Labor-Supply Wedge from Subsistence-Routed Distribution

detail.title: The Unpriced Value of Time: A Labor-Supply Wedge from Subsistence-Routed Distribution
detail.abstract: The wage performs two functions at once: it prices labor and it is, for most households, the only channel through which the economy delivers a claim on output. We show that bundling distribution into the price corrupts the price. When subsistence is reachable only by selling labor, low-wage labor supply is a constrained corner rather than an interior optimum, and the marginal rate of substitution between consumption and non-market time exceeds the wage by a wedge τ ≥ 0. Proposition 1 establishes that this wedge is not identified from labor-market data and that the standard practice of valuing labor's opportunity cost at the market wage returns the infimum of the identified set, a lower bound of known sign. Proposition 2 traces the allocative consequence: value-destroying activities are undertaken whenever their social product exceeds w rather than w + τ , so the wedge equals the width of the resulting "make-work" band, which widens under labor-substituting automation. Proposition 3 then shows the wedge to be a cost-benefit inefficiency whose realisation is, through the subsistence floor, a distributive act: by the compensating-variation criterion the wage-routed regime is inefficient, yet it sits on the Pareto frontier, so the loss is neither purely efficiency nor purely equity but the two conflated. Funding the floor from a tax on inelastic factors recovers the cost-benefit gain while shifting incidence onto the rent base.

detail.abstract: India's Phillips curve has looked at the familiar missing relationship across 1997-2025, a period that spans the 2016 adoption of flexible inflation targeting and is dominated by recurrent supply shocks. We ask whether that flatness survives once demand and supply disturbances are separated and whether the Reserve Bank of India's own account of each quarter agrees. We measure the demand supply split three ways: a mechanical inflation with output-gap co-movement rule; a gap-blind reading of the Reserve Bank's quarterly assessments by a large language model (LLM) under a fixed, pre-specified protocol; and the Bank's revealed practice. The pooled output-gap slope is statistically zero, but this is an artefact of pooling disturbances: conditioning on the shock, the demand-pull slope is +2.2 before targeting and switches off to zero after it, while the supply-driven (cost-push) slope stays negative throughout the signature of a central bank that offsets demand before it reaches prices. Read independently of the gap, the language model recovers the same regime contrast, reading 77 of 115 quarters as supply-led with demand a frequent co-driver; three independent model families agree on the classification (Fleiss κ = 0.45). The paper's contribution is to identify which channel flattened, and to scale the narrative identification of supply and demand shocks with a hybrid design that leaves the econometrics classical and uses the language model only to read the policy record at scale.

title: Nigeria’s Anti-Money Laundering Framework: A Critical Assessment of Regulatory Defeicencies and Institutional Challenges

detail.title: Nigeria’s Anti-Money Laundering Framework: A Critical Assessment of Regulatory Defeicencies and Institutional Challenges
detail.abstract: Nigeria's anti-money laundering (AML) regime occupies a significant position in the fight against organised crime, corruption, and terrorism financing. Notwithstanding an increasingly elaborate legal framework, its operational effectiveness remains constrained by persistent institutional and regulatory deficiencies. This study undertakes a doctrinal and policy-oriented examination of Nigeria's AML framework, interrogating the coherence of its statutory instruments and the functional capacity of key enforcement bodies, including the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, and the judiciary. Drawing on contemporary reports and regulatory practice, the analysis reveals structural incoherence, overlapping mandates, and weak inter-agency coordination as central impediments to effective enforcement. It further identifies capacity deficits, resource constraints, and undue political influence as factors that compromise institutional independence and prosecutorial efficacy. The study contends that, absent targeted legislative reform and strengthened accountability mechanisms, Nigeria's AML framework will remain largely reactive, with limited preventive impact. It advances reform proposals aimed at enhancing regulatory clarity, institutional synergy, and compliance with international standards. By situating these challenges within general debates on governance and legal effectiveness in emerging economies, the study contributes to ongoing efforts to reimagine AML enforcement as a proactive and resilient component of criminal justice administration in Nigeria.

title: Double Machine Learning Meets Hierarchical Bayes

detail.title: Double Machine Learning Meets Hierarchical Bayes
detail.abstract: Double Machine Learning (DML) and Hierarchical Bayes share a common object: the nuisance function. DML uses machine learning to estimate nuisances and achieves √ nconsistent causal inference via Neyman-orthogonal cross-fitting. The horseshoe prior (Carvalho, Polson, and Scott, 2010) provides near-minimax nuisance regularisation through the Adaptive Bayes Oracle Shrinkage (ABOS) theorem of Datta and Ghosh (2013), with half-Cauchy local scales that stabilise inverse propensity weights without trimming. We embed horseshoe-regularised nuisances within the DML cross-fitting framework to obtain a Bayesian AIPW-DML estimator (B-AIPW-DML) that is doubly robust, √ n-normal under a trilinear rate condition, and consistent where standard DML fails: under dense confounding, near-overlap violation, and missing-at-random panel dropout. The last connects to the Rathouz (2004) modified conditional likelihood, which we embed in a doubly robust panel score whose trilinear rate condition relaxes the standard DML bilinear requirement whenever the dropout mechanism is sparse. Four simulation designs and a Lalonde wage application confirm the theory.

title: On the Trade-Off Between Calibration and Discrimination in Credit Risk Modeling: A Financial Value Perspective
